title: A balanced diet: why your body needs many kinds of food

summary.text: A plate of rice can fill your stomach and still leave your body short of protein, iron and vitamins. A balanced diet means eating many kinds of food, in about the right amounts, over a day or a week. Inside you, food is broken down into tiny building blocks, and your blood carries them to about 30 trillion cells. Your cells burn some of them for energy and use the rest to grow and mend. About as many microbes live in your gut, and they eat the fibre you cannot digest. No single food is good or bad on its own, because what matters is the mix over many meals.
summary.art: A steel thali seen from above, half green with poriyal and fruit, a quarter golden with rice and chapati, a quarter red-brown with dal and curd, a glass of water beside it, and faint dotted lines running from each part to a tiny glowing cell.

intro.hook: Breathe out slowly onto your hand. Feel how warm it is. Part of that breath is the chapati or rice you ate yesterday. How did your food get into your breath?
intro.text: Almost all our food starts as plants growing in sunlight. Here we follow it after you swallow it. A spoon of dal does not stay dal for long. It is broken into pieces far too small to see. Then it travels in your blood to every part of you. Some of it becomes your muscles and your hair. Some of it is burned for energy, and you breathe it out. Some of it feeds trillions of tiny living things in your gut. So why do we need so many kinds of food? Why not just eat rice, or just eat sweets?
intro.art: A girl breathing out onto her palm, a faint curl of warm breath, and inside a dotted outline of her body a tiny chapati breaking into sparkling specks that flow to her lungs.

outcomes: I can say what a balanced diet is: many kinds of food, in about the right amounts, over a day or a week.
I can sort foods into energy foods, body-building foods and protecting foods, and know that many foods do more than one job.
I can make a balanced plate or thali from the food in my own kitchen.
I can explain that food is broken into tiny building blocks, carried by the blood to my cells, and used for energy and for building.
I can explain why my body needs each kind of food: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.
I can run a fair test, count or measure the results, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that trillions of microbes live in my gut and eat the fibre I cannot digest.
I can say what scientists agree on about diets, and what they still argue about, without calling any food or person good or bad.

terms.meaning: All the food and drink a person usually has. It does not mean eating less.
terms.example: A family in Kerala and a family in Punjab may have very different diets. Both can be healthy.
terms.art: Two family meals side by side: appam with stew and a banana leaf, and makki roti with sarson saag and lassi.

terms.meaning: Eating many kinds of food in about the right amounts, over a day or a week, so the body gets everything it needs.
terms.example: Idli and sambar for breakfast, rice, dal and poriyal (cooked vegetables) for lunch, a guava after school and chapati with egg curry or paneer at night.
terms.art: A day drawn as four small plates in a row, each a different colour mix, adding up to one rainbow.

terms.meaning: A part of food that the body uses to live, grow and stay well.
terms.example: Protein in dal, calcium in milk and vitamin C in amla are all nutrients.
terms.art: A bowl of dal with tiny labelled specks rising out of it: protein, iron, fibre.

terms.meaning: Foods that give the body most of its energy. Rice, chapati, millets, potatoes, bananas, sugar and fats are energy foods.
terms.example: A plate of upma gives you energy to run to the park.
terms.art: A golden plate of rice, chapati, ragi mudde and a banana, with little lightning marks above them.

terms.meaning: Foods with lots of protein. The body uses protein to build and mend itself.
terms.example: Dal, rajma, chana, sprouts, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish, meat and peanuts.
terms.art: A red-brown plate with a bowl of dal, a boiled egg, a cube of paneer and some peanuts, beside a child measuring her height.

terms.meaning: Vegetables and fruits. They give vitamins, minerals and fibre, which help every part of the body work and stay well.
terms.example: Palak, carrots, tomatoes, guava, amla and papaya.
terms.art: A green plate piled with palak, carrot sticks, tomato, guava and a slice of papaya, with a soft glow around it.

terms.meaning: A nutrient made of sugars. Sugar, starch and fibre are all carbohydrates. Sugar and starch give the body most of its energy.
terms.example: Rice and chapati are mostly a carbohydrate called starch.
terms.art: A grain of rice zoomed in to show it is packed with tiny chains of beads.

terms.meaning: A long chain of sugar pieces joined together. Plants store their energy as starch.
terms.example: When you chew a piece of chapati for a long time, it starts to taste a little sweet. Your spit is cutting the starch into sugar.
terms.art: A long necklace of identical beads, with one bead snipped off by tiny scissors.

terms.meaning: The simple sugar that your cells use for energy. Starch is broken into glucose inside you.
terms.example: Your blood carries glucose to your brain all day and all night.
terms.art: A tiny six-cornered shape floating in a red river towards a brain.

terms.meaning: A long chain made of building blocks called amino acids. Your muscles, hair, skin and blood are built with proteins.
terms.example: Your hair and nails are made mostly of a protein called keratin.
terms.art: A coloured bead chain folding itself into a knot, next to a strand of hair.

terms.meaning: The building blocks of proteins. There are about 20 kinds. Your body joins them in new orders to make its own proteins.
terms.example: The amino acids in dal are joined again inside you to make your own muscle.
terms.art: Twenty differently coloured beads in a row, a child's hand joining them into a new chain.

terms.meaning: An oily nutrient. It carries a lot of energy. It also builds the thin skin around every cell, called the cell membrane, and helps the body take in some vitamins.
terms.example: Ghee, oil, butter, coconut and peanuts all have fat.
terms.art: A drop of oil next to a cell, with the cell's thin outer skin drawn as a ring of tiny oily beads.

terms.meaning: A nutrient the body needs in very small amounts to work properly. Each vitamin has its own jobs.
terms.example: Vitamin C in amla and guava helps your body mend cuts.
terms.art: A pinch of sparkle above an amla, much smaller than the amla itself.

terms.meaning: A nutrient that comes from rocks and soil, through plants and animals into us. Calcium and iron are minerals.
terms.example: Calcium from milk, ragi and til builds your bones.
terms.art: A rock, a ragi plant growing from soil, and a child's bone, joined by arrows.

terms.meaning: A mineral that the blood uses to carry oxygen around the body.
terms.example: Dal, palak, rajma, bajra, eggs and meat all have iron.
terms.art: A red blood cell drawn as a tiny cushion carrying little oxygen bubbles.

terms.meaning: A mineral that makes bones and teeth hard. It also helps muscles and nerves work.
terms.example: Milk, curd, paneer, ragi, til and green leaves have calcium.
terms.art: A child's skeleton outline with bones glowing white, a glass of milk and a ragi ball beside it.

terms.meaning: A kind of carbohydrate in plant foods that your body cannot break down. It keeps food moving through your gut and feeds your gut microbes.
terms.example: The skin of an apple, the green skin on whole moong and the strings in beans and bhindi are fibre.
terms.art: A peeled-back apple skin and a bowl of whole moong, with tiny threads drawn in them.

terms.meaning: Breaking food into pieces small enough to pass into the blood.
terms.example: Digestion starts in your mouth when you chew, and goes on in your stomach and intestines.
terms.art: A simple outline of the gut from mouth to large intestine, with a chapati getting smaller at each stage.

terms.meaning: A kind of protein that cuts big pieces of food into smaller ones, very fast. It works like tiny scissors.
terms.example: An enzyme in your spit cuts starch into sugar.
terms.art: Tiny scissors with a smiling outline cutting a bead necklace.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that every living thing is made of. Your body has about 30 trillion cells.
terms.example: Skin cells, muscle cells, blood cells and brain cells are all cells, each with their own job.
terms.art: A crowd of different cells: a round red blood cell, a long muscle cell, a branching nerve cell, a flat skin cell.

terms.meaning: Tiny parts inside your cells that burn food with oxygen to release energy.
terms.example: Your muscle cells are full of mitochondria. That is why they can work so hard.
terms.art: A cell cut open, with bean-shaped mitochondria glowing inside them.

terms.meaning: The trillions of tiny living things, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut, most of all in the large intestine.
terms.example: Gut microbes eat the fibre from your dal and poriyal, which you cannot digest yourself.
terms.art: A busy crowd of different-shaped bacteria inside a curved tube, some munching on threads of fibre.

terms.meaning: A unit for measuring the energy in food. One kilocalorie is the energy needed to warm 1 litre of water by 1 degree Celsius. Food labels write it as kcal. People often just say 'calories'.
terms.example: A banana gives roughly 100 kcal. A child of eight uses very roughly 1,500 to 2,000 kcal in a day.
terms.art: A banana on a weighing scale whose dial reads energy instead of weight.

terms.meaning: When the body is not getting enough of one nutrient for a long time. It can make people ill.
terms.example: Too little vitamin C for many weeks causes an illness called scurvy.
terms.art: A plant with yellow leaves in a pot next to a healthy green one, both with their roots showing.

explanations.definition: A balanced diet is eating many kinds of food, in about the right amounts, over a day or a week. It gives the body all the nutrients it needs, plus enough water.
explanations.description: Your body needs many different things from food. No single food has all of them. Rice gives lots of energy but little calcium. Milk gives calcium but almost no vitamin C. Amla is full of vitamin C but gives little energy. So we eat many kinds. A balanced diet does not mean every meal must be perfect. A festival plate of sweets is fine. What matters is the mix over many days. Balanced also does not mean eating less. Growing children need plenty of food.
examples: A day of idli and sambar, rice with dal and poriyal, a guava, and chapati with egg curry is balanced. It has energy foods, body-building foods and protecting foods.
Eating only rice and pickle for weeks is not balanced. The body would miss protein, vitamins and minerals, even though the stomach feels full.
One plate of jalebis at a wedding does not make a diet unbalanced. A diet is what you usually eat.
explanations.art: A week drawn as seven small thalis in a row, each slightly different, with a big rainbow arching over all seven.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a balanced diet is, and what it is not.

explanations.concept: Go, grow and glow: three jobs food does
explanations.definition: Energy foods (go foods) give the body fuel. Body-building foods (grow foods) give protein to build and mend. Protecting foods (glow foods) give vitamins, minerals and fibre that keep the body working well.
explanations.description: An easy way to plan a meal is to think of three jobs. Go foods are rice, chapati, millets like ragi and bajra, potatoes and bananas. Grow foods are dal, chana, rajma, sprouts, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish, meat and nuts. Glow foods are vegetables and fruits. Water and a little fat are needed too. Many foods do more than one job. Dal gives protein and also fibre and iron. Peanuts give protein, fat and energy. Milk gives protein and calcium. So the groups are a helpful map, not strict boxes. Different countries draw them differently. Some use five groups, some use a plate and some used a pyramid.
examples: A lunch of rice (go), dal (grow) and bhindi poriyal (glow) does all three jobs.
Egg bhurji with chapati and tomato does all three jobs too.
A plate of rice and potato curry is mostly go. Adding a bowl of curd and a cucumber adds grow and glow.
explanations.art: Three friendly signposts: a golden one with a running shoe, a red-brown one with a measuring tape, and a green one with a shining shield.
explanations.context: This card explains a simple way of sorting food into three jobs, so you can plan a balanced plate.

explanations.concept: The balanced plate: how much of each
explanations.definition: About half of a balanced plate is vegetables and fruits. About a quarter is grains or millets. The last quarter is dal, milk foods, eggs, fish, meat or nuts. Water is the drink.
explanations.description: Nutrition scientists in many countries draw a healthy meal as a plate. India's National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad uses one called 'My Plate for the Day' in its 2024 food guide. Like many others, it gives about half the plate to vegetables and fruits. Grains and millets take about a quarter. Pulses, milk foods, eggs, fish, meat and nuts take the rest. Fats and oils come in small amounts. Many Indian homes already eat this way. A thali has small bowls of dal, poriyal, curd and chutney around rice or chapati. A banana-leaf meal in the south puts many small heaps of vegetables around the rice. One-pot foods count too. Khichdi with vegetables, or a biryani with raita and salad, can be balanced.
examples: A thali with a big helping of poriyal and salad, one chapati and some rice, a bowl of dal and a bowl of curd.
A Kerala sadya on a banana leaf has many vegetable dishes like avial, thoran and olan around the rice.
Vegetable khichdi with a spoon of ghee and a bowl of curd is a balanced one-pot meal.
explanations.art: A round steel thali divided into a big green half, a golden quarter and a red-brown quarter, with a glass of water at the side.
explanations.context: This card shows how much of each kind of food a balanced plate usually has.

explanations.concept: What happens to food inside you: digestion
explanations.definition: Digestion is breaking food into pieces small enough to pass through the wall of the gut into the blood.
explanations.description: Food goes on a long trip through a tube called the gut. In your mouth, teeth crush it and spit wets it. An enzyme in your spit starts cutting starch into sugar. In your stomach, strong acid and more enzymes break proteins apart. The stomach churns the food into a thick soup. In the small intestine, juices from the pancreas take over. They cut starch into glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into smaller pieces. Bile from the liver breaks fat into tiny drops so the enzymes can reach it. Then those tiny pieces pass through the intestine wall into the blood. Whatever is left, mostly fibre and water, moves on to the large intestine. There the gut microbes get to work.
examples: A chapati becomes glucose. A spoon of dal becomes amino acids. A drop of ghee becomes fatty acids.
Vitamins and minerals do not need to be cut up. They are already small enough to pass into the blood.
The small intestine of a grown-up is several metres long. Laid out straight, it would stretch past two grown-ups lying head to toe.
explanations.art: A simple gut drawn as a winding road from mouth to large intestine, with a chapati, an egg and a dal bowl at the start, and small coloured beads at the end flowing into a red river.
explanations.context: This card explains how the body breaks food into tiny building blocks, step by step.

explanations.concept: Your food travels to 30 trillion cells
explanations.definition: After digestion, the blood carries the tiny food pieces to every cell in the body. Each cell takes what they need.
explanations.description: Your body is made of about 30 trillion cells. That is 30 followed by twelve zeros. Each one is alive and needs food. Your heart pumps blood past almost every cell, all the time. The blood carries glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. A muscle cell takes amino acids to build more muscle. A bone cell takes calcium. A cell in the bone marrow takes iron and folate to make new red blood cells. A brain cell takes glucose. Your body is always rebuilding itself like this. The lining of your gut is replaced every few days. So part of you next month will be built from this month's food.
examples: Your red blood cells each live about four months. New ones are made all the time from the iron, protein and vitamins in your food.
When you grow taller, your bone cells are using calcium and protein from your food.
Even while you sleep, your brain uses glucose from your dinner.
explanations.art: A red river of blood flowing past a row of different cells, each reaching out to take a different coloured bead: a muscle cell taking red beads, a bone cell white, a brain cell gold.
explanations.context: This card follows food after digestion: how the blood carries it to every cell in the body.

explanations.concept: Inside the cell: food plus oxygen gives energy
explanations.definition: Inside each cell, tiny parts called mitochondria join glucose or fat with oxygen. This releases the energy the cell uses. Carbon dioxide and water are left over.
explanations.description: Your cells need energy for everything: moving, growing, thinking and keeping warm. They get it by slowly burning food with oxygen. It is a bit like a fire. But it happens gently, in tiny steps, so it never gets hot enough to hurt. This is why you breathe. You breathe in oxygen for your cells. You breathe out the carbon dioxide they made from your food. When the body burns its stored fat, most of that fat leaves through the breath, as carbon dioxide. Two scientists in Australia worked this out in 2014. The brain is very hungry. In a child of about five, the brain uses nearly half of all the energy the body burns.
examples: Run fast and you breathe harder. Your muscle cells are burning more food and need more oxygen.
Your body stays at about 37 degrees Celsius. That warmth comes from your cells burning food.
Breathe out onto a cold mirror. The mist is partly water made from your food.
explanations.art: A cell cut open, their bean-shaped mitochondria glowing, a glucose bead and two oxygen bubbles going in, a little carbon dioxide puff and a water drop coming out.
explanations.context: This card goes inside a single cell, to see how food becomes energy.

explanations.definition: Carbohydrates, like starch and sugar, are the body's main fuel. They are broken into glucose, which every cell can burn for energy.
explanations.description: Rice, chapati, ragi, jowar, bajra, poha, potatoes and bananas are mostly starch. Starch is a long chain of glucose pieces. Your body cuts the chain and sends the glucose into the blood. Whole grains are cut more slowly than white rice or maida, especially when you eat them with dal and vegetables. Then the glucose comes in a gentle stream. Sugar and sweets need very little cutting, so their glucose arrives in a rush. Your body can handle that sometimes. But lots of added sugar every day feeds the mouth bacteria that make holes in teeth. Over many years, eating a lot of added sugar is also linked to illnesses such as diabetes. Any extra glucose that is not needed is stored, first in the liver and muscles, then as fat.
examples: Chapati made from whole atta, eaten with dal and poriyal, gives a steady stream of energy through the afternoon.
A glass of sugary sharbat gives a quick rush of energy.
Chew a piece of chapati thirty times. It starts to taste sweet as your spit cuts starch into sugar.
explanations.art: A slow, steady stream of golden beads flowing from a plate of chapati, dal and poriyal, beside a sudden splash of beads from a glass of sharbat.
explanations.context: This card explains why we need energy foods like rice, chapati and millets.

explanations.concept: Why the body needs protein, and why dal and rice go together
explanations.definition: Proteins are long chains of about 20 kinds of building blocks called amino acids. The body breaks food proteins into amino acids, then joins them in new orders to build its own proteins.
explanations.description: Your muscles, skin, hair, nails, blood and enzymes are made of proteins. They wear out and are rebuilt all the time, and children are also growing. So you need protein every day. Your body can make some amino acids itself. But there are nine kinds it cannot make. They must come from food. Eggs, milk, fish and meat have all nine in good amounts. Grains like rice and wheat are a little low in one, called lysine. Dals and beans are a little low in another, called methionine. Eaten over the same day, they fill each other's gaps. That is one reason dal-chawal, rajma-chawal, idli-sambar and chapati-chana are such good pairs.
examples: Idli is made from rice and urad dal ground together. So every idli has grain protein and dal protein, and they fill each other's gaps.
A vegetarian family can get all the protein a child needs from dals, beans, milk, curd, paneer, nuts and grains.
Your hair is mostly a protein called keratin. When you grow it longer, you are using protein from your food.
explanations.art: A bowl of rice and a bowl of dal, each with a bead chain missing one colour, and the two chains together showing every colour.
explanations.context: This card explains why the body needs protein, and why pulses and grains eaten together give the body a better mix.

explanations.definition: Fat carries the most energy of any nutrient. It also builds the thin skin around every cell, called the cell membrane. And it helps the body take in vitamins A, D, E and K.
explanations.description: Fat is often talked about as if it were only a problem. But the body cannot live without it. Every one of your 30 trillion cells is wrapped in a thin skin made largely of fats. A large part of your brain is made of fat. Carrots and palak have beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A. Beta-carotene and vitamin A dissolve in fat. That is why a little oil or ghee in the cooking helps you take in more of them. Fat in the body also stores energy and keeps you warm. Scientists do argue about which fats are best, and how much of each. You will meet that argument on another card.
examples: Peanuts, til, coconut, ghee and mustard oil all carry fat.
Carrots cooked with a little oil give your body more beta-carotene, and so more vitamin A, than raw carrots with no fat at all.
Fish from the sea, walnuts and flax seeds have a kind of fat called omega-3 that the brain uses.
explanations.art: A cell membrane drawn as two rows of tiny beads with tails, all lined up like a fence, next to a spoon of ghee and a handful of peanuts.
explanations.context: This card explains why the body needs fat, even though people often talk about fat as a problem.

explanations.concept: Vitamins and minerals: tiny amounts, big jobs
explanations.definition: Vitamins and minerals are nutrients the body needs in very small amounts. Without them, many parts of the body slowly stop working well.
explanations.description: You need only a pinch of each vitamin and mineral, but you need them every week. Vitamin C, in amla, guava, lemon and oranges, helps make skin, gums and blood vessels strong. It also helps the body take in iron from plant foods. Iron, in dal, palak, bajra, rajma, eggs and meat, goes into the blood to carry oxygen. Calcium, in milk, curd, ragi, til and green leaves, makes bones hard. Iodine, in iodised salt and sea fish, helps the body grow and the brain develop. Vitamin D is made in your own skin when sunlight falls on it. Folate, in green leaves, dals and yeast, helps make new blood cells. Many of them were discovered when people fell ill without them.
examples: Squeeze lemon on your dal. The vitamin C helps you take in the dal's iron.
Sailors on long voyages used to fall ill with scurvy. In 1747 a ship's doctor, James Lind, showed that oranges and lemons cured it. We now know the cure is vitamin C.
Since 1962, India has worked to add iodine to salt. This has prevented a swelling of the neck called goitre in millions of people.
explanations.art: A row of tiny jars labelled with letters and names, each with a small picture of its job: a mended cut, a red blood cell, a strong bone, a growing child, a sun on skin.
explanations.context: This card explains vitamins and minerals, which the body needs in tiny amounts.

explanations.concept: Fibre and the trillions of microbes in your gut
explanations.definition: Fibre is the part of plant food that your body cannot digest. In the large intestine, trillions of gut microbes eat it. They make substances that help feed the cells of your gut.
explanations.description: Your large intestine is home to roughly as many bacteria as there are cells in your whole body. That is tens of trillions. There are hundreds of different kinds. They are living things with their own lives, not just helpers. They live in a warm, dark tube with food arriving several times a day. Their favourite food is the fibre you cannot break down, from dal husks, whole grains, vegetables and fruit. As they eat it, they make gas, which is why rajma and chana can make you fart. They also make small acids. One, called butyrate, is the main food of the cells lining your large intestine. So you feed them, and they feed you back. People who eat many kinds of plants tend to have more kinds of gut microbes. Scientists are still finding out what that means for health.
examples: Rajma and chana can make a lot of gas. Your gut microbes make that gas as they eat the fibre.
The Hadza people of Tanzania hunt and gather their food. Their gut microbes change with the seasons, as their food changes.
Curd contains living microbes. Most of them pass through, but some may help while they are inside you.
explanations.art: A cosy curved tunnel full of many differently shaped and coloured bacteria eating threads of fibre, with small bubbles of gas and tiny gift parcels passing to the tunnel wall.
explanations.context: This card is about the fibre in food and the microbes in your gut that eat it.

explanations.definition: Water is a nutrient. It makes up more than half of your body weight. Blood, spit, digestive juices and the inside of every cell are mostly water.
explanations.description: You lose water all day, in your breath, sweat and urine. So you need to drink it back, as plain water, milk, buttermilk, dal and the water in fruit and vegetables. When you do not drink enough, you feel tired and can get headaches. Children playing in Indian summers can lose a lot in sweat. A simple check is the colour of your urine. Pale yellow usually means you are drinking enough. Dark yellow means drink more. A person can live only a few days without water, but weeks without food.
examples: A glass of buttermilk on a hot day gives water, protein and calcium together.
A watermelon is about nine-tenths water.
After a cricket match in May, your shirt is wet with sweat. That water must be drunk back.
explanations.art: A clay matka with a steel tumbler, a slice of watermelon and a glass of chaas, beside a child's outline filled more than halfway with blue.
explanations.context: This card explains why water is part of a balanced diet.

explanations.concept: A healthy diet and a less healthy diet
explanations.description: Scientists agree on a lot. Diets with plenty of vegetables, fruits, pulses, whole grains and nuts are linked to good health in many countries. Some diets have lots of added sugar, salt and very processed packet foods, and few vegetables. They are linked to more tooth decay, and over many years to heart illness. But they do not agree on everything. They argue about which fats are best, about eggs, and about why packet foods seem to make people eat more. And very different traditional diets have kept people healthy. No single food makes a diet healthy or unhealthy. It is the pattern over years.
examples: Eating sweets after every meal, every day, gives mouth bacteria a steady supply of sugar. They make acid that eats holes in teeth.
A diet of the same few foods, day after day, can miss a vitamin even when the stomach is always full.
A family that eats home-cooked dal, rice, poriyal and curd most days, with sweets on festivals, has a healthy pattern.

perspectives.who: Most nutrition scientists, and the World Health Organization
perspectives.explanation: Eat mostly vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses and nuts. Keep added sugar under a tenth of your food energy, and less is better. Use less salt. This advice is based on studies of millions of people.

perspectives.who: Carlos Monteiro and colleagues in Brazil, from 2009
perspectives.explanation: The problem is not one nutrient but how food is made. 'Ultra-processed' packet foods, made in factories from many added ingredients, may cause people to eat more than they need. In a careful 2019 test in the United States, people ate about 500 kcal more each day on such foods. Others say the label is too broad, because it puts very different foods together.

Healthy diets come in very different shapes. Some traditional diets have kept people well with lots of fish and fat, others with lots of rice and vegetables, and others with lots of milk. So we should be careful about one rule for everyone.

explanations.art: Two long ribbons of a year of meals: one with many colours mixed through it, and one mostly one colour with a few sparks of other colours.
explanations.context: This card compares healthy and less healthy diets, and says where scientists still disagree.

explanations.description: A balanced diet is not one fixed menu. A baby, a growing child, a pregnant mother, a farmer and an old grandparent need different amounts. Some bodies also digest foods differently. Most people in the world digest milk sugar less well once they grow up. Some get tummy aches from milk. In India, this is more common in the south and east than in the north-west. Some people cannot eat wheat, or peanuts. Families also choose foods because of their beliefs. Some eat no meat, Jain families eat no root vegetables, and some eat no beef or pork. A balanced diet can be built inside all of these. Scientists are now asking a newer question. Why does the same food raise one person's blood sugar a lot, and another's only a little?
examples: A Jain family eats no root vegetables like onion and potato. They can still balance their plate with dals, milk foods, grains, leafy greens and fruit.
A cousin who gets tummy aches from milk can have curd, which has less milk sugar, or ragi and til for calcium.
A grandmother and a growing ten-year-old may eat the same dal, but need different amounts.

perspectives.explanation: General rules work well for most people: a mix of food groups, enough protein for growth, lots of vegetables, and not too much added sugar or salt.

perspectives.who: Eran Segal, Eran Elinav and colleagues, Israel, 2015
perspectives.explanation: They measured the blood sugar of 800 people after meals. The same food raised it very differently in different people. Their gut microbes seemed to be part of the reason. They think diets may one day be planned for each person. Other scientists say this is promising but not yet proven.

explanations.art: A big family table with plates of different shapes and sizes: a baby's small bowl, a child's thali, a grandfather's plate, all with a bit of each colour.
explanations.context: This card is about how different people need different plates, and what scientists are still finding out.

agreed.text: The body needs many different nutrients, and no single food has all of them in the right amounts.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the nutrients in thousands of foods. In India, C. Gopalan and his colleagues at the National Institute of Nutrition published these measurements for Indian foods from 1971, in a book called 'Nutritive Value of Indian Foods'.

agreed.text: Food is broken into small building blocks, which pass into the blood and are carried to the cells.
agreed.evidence: Doctors can measure glucose and amino acids rising in the blood after a meal. A simple finger-prick test shows blood sugar going up after eating rice.

agreed.text: Missing one vitamin or mineral for a long time causes a particular illness, and eating it again cures it.
agreed.evidence: Scurvy is cured by vitamin C, beriberi by vitamin B1, and one kind of anaemia by folate. These cures have been tested in careful trials since James Lind's test on sailors in 1747.

agreed.text: Sugar eaten often helps mouth bacteria make acid that causes holes in teeth.
agreed.evidence: Studies across many countries and many years show that people who eat sugar more often get more tooth decay. Bacteria in the mouth can be watched turning sugar into acid in the laboratory.

agreed.text: Tens of trillions of microbes live in the human gut, mostly in the large intestine. They digest fibre that we cannot.
agreed.evidence: Scientists count them by looking at stool samples and reading their genes. In 2016, Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo estimated about 38 trillion bacteria, roughly as many as the body's own cells.

challenging.claim: Some foods are 'good' and some foods are 'bad'.
challenging.who: A very common way of talking about food, in homes, schools and adverts
challenging.for: Some foods, like vegetables and dals, give the body a lot that it needs. Others, like sweets and fried snacks, mostly give quick energy, fat or salt.
challenging.against: Nutrition scientists look at the whole diet, not one food. A laddoo at Deepavali does no harm in a balanced diet. And even 'good' foods can be too much: a diet of only spinach would miss protein and energy. Calling foods bad can also make children feel ashamed of what they eat, or of what their family can afford.
challenging.context: This card looks at the idea that foods can be sorted into good and bad.

challenging.claim: Fat in food is the main cause of heart disease, so eat as little fat as possible.
challenging.who: The American scientist Ancel Keys, from the 1950s, and many food guides in the 1980s and 1990s
challenging.for: Some studies linked diets high in certain fats, like those in butter and meat, with more heart disease.
challenging.against: The British scientist John Yudkin argued that sugar was a bigger problem, in his 1972 book 'Pure, White and Deadly'. He was mocked at the time. In 2016, researchers found papers showing that a sugar industry group had paid Harvard scientists in the 1960s to play down sugar's role. Today most scientists think the kind of fat matters more than the amount, and that added sugar also matters.
challenging.context: This card is about a long argument over whether fat or sugar is the bigger worry for the heart.

challenging.claim: Vegetarians must eat dal and rice in the same meal to get complete protein.
challenging.who: Frances Moore Lappé, in her famous 1971 book 'Diet for a Small Planet'
challenging.for: Grains and pulses each lack enough of one amino acid. Together they make up the full set.
challenging.against: Lappé herself said in the 1981 edition that strict combining at every meal was not needed. The body keeps a pool of amino acids, so eating grains and pulses over the same day is enough. She changed her mind when the evidence changed, which is what careful thinkers do.
challenging.context: This card is about an old rule for vegetarian meals, and the scientist who changed her own mind about it.

challenging.claim: Eating curd, or taking 'good bacteria' pills, makes you healthy and helps you live longer.
challenging.who: The Russian scientist Ilya Mechnikov, in his 1907 book 'The Prolongation of Life', and many adverts today
challenging.for: Mechnikov noticed that some villagers in Bulgaria who drank soured milk lived long lives. Some trials show certain microbes can help with some kinds of diarrhoea.
challenging.against: Most microbes in curd or pills pass through the gut and do not stay. The long-lived villagers may have been healthy for many other reasons. Many claims on packets go far beyond the evidence. Curd is a good food, but not a magic one.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that eating living microbes keeps you healthy.

challenging.claim: The vitamins were discovered by a few famous men.
challenging.who: Many history books, and the 1929 Nobel Prize, which went to Christiaan Eijkman and Frederick Gowland Hopkins
challenging.for: Eijkman found that chickens fed white polished rice got a nerve illness that unpolished rice cured. Hopkins showed that rats needed tiny 'extra' food factors to grow.
challenging.against: Gerrit Grijns, who worked with Eijkman, was the first to say clearly that a missing nutrient caused the illness, but he got no prize. Lucy Wills, working in Bombay from 1928, found a cure for an anaemia of pregnant women that led to the discovery of folate. Elsie Widdowson measured the nutrients in British foods from the 1930s. Kamala Sohonie, the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, later studied the food value of neera, a palm drink, for children. Discoveries are usually made by many people, and not all of them are remembered.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering vitamins and the science of nutrition.

challenging.claim: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
challenging.who: A common saying, used a lot in cereal adverts since the early 1900s
challenging.for: Many children who eat breakfast pay attention better in the morning. School breakfast and lunch schemes help children who would otherwise be hungry.
challenging.against: In studies of adults, skipping breakfast has not clearly made people less healthy. What matters most is the whole day's food. The saying was spread partly by companies selling breakfast cereal. For growing children, eating regular meals still matters.
challenging.context: This card looks at a common saying about breakfast, and what the evidence says.

big_questions.q: If your body is rebuilt from your food, are you the same person you were a year ago?
big_questions.hint: Your red blood cells last about four months. Your gut lining lasts a few days. But you still remember last year.

big_questions.q: Your gut microbes eat the fibre you cannot digest, and feed your gut cells in return. Are they part of you, or guests?
big_questions.hint: They have their own lives and their own genes. But you could not be healthy without them.

big_questions.q: Why can the body make some amino acids but not others?
big_questions.hint: Our far-back ancestors ate plants and animals that already had them. What happens to a skill you never need to use?

big_questions.q: When you breathe out, you breathe out part of your dinner. Where does that breath go next?
big_questions.hint: Carbon dioxide is what plants take in to make their food.

big_questions.q: Why do some children in India not get a balanced diet? Is that their family's fault?
big_questions.hint: Think about prices, money, distance to a market, and who gets to eat first in a home. Since 2001, India's Supreme Court has said every child in a government primary school must get a cooked lunch.

big_questions.q: Grandparents in many places ate ragi, jowar and bajra. Why did many families stop, and why are some now starting again?
big_questions.hint: Ask an elder. The United Nations called 2023 the International Year of Millets, after India asked for it.

big_questions.q: Should we choose our food only for our own health, or also for the animals, the farmers and the Earth?
big_questions.hint: Every plate has a story behind it: soil, water, animals and people's work.

big_questions.q: Who decides what a 'healthy' plate looks like, and could they be wrong?
big_questions.hint: The food pyramids of the 1990s told people to eat 6 to 11 servings of grain a day. The advice later changed.

big_questions.q: If no food is bad on its own, why do adverts and labels make some foods look so tempting?
big_questions.hint: Who earns money when you buy a packet? Who earns money when you buy a bunch of methi?

story.title: The Brown Jar
story.note: Lucy Wills (1888 to 1964) was a real British doctor and scientist. From 1928 she worked in Bombay, studying a dangerous anaemia in pregnant women who worked in the textile mills. She noticed that richer women rarely got it, so she suspected their food. She tested diets on animals in her laboratory, then found that Marmite, a cheap spread made from yeast left over from brewing, cured the women. She published this in the British Medical Journal in 1931. The missing nutrient, first called the 'Wills factor', was later named folic acid, or folate, in 1941, after it was found in spinach leaves. Kamal, her mother, the nurse, how Dr Wills looks, the conversations, the microscope scene and the methi tin are made up.
text: In the winter of 1929, in the city of Bombay, my mother began to turn the colour of the moon.

My name is Kamal. I was ten. We lived in one room of a chawl in Parel, on the third floor, where the mill whistle woke us before the crows did. My mother, Sakhu, worked at a spinning machine in the cotton mill, twelve hours a day. There was a baby growing inside her. And every week she grew paler.

First it was her lips. Then it was the inside of her eyelids, which should be red like a guava and were white like a radish. On the stairs she stopped at every landing, holding the rail, breathing as if she had run all the way from the sea. 'It is nothing,' she said. 'It is the cotton dust.' Our neighbour said it was the heat. Another said it was the evil eye, and tied a black thread on Aai's wrist.

I carried her tiffin to the mill gate at noon. It was always the same. Rice, a little thin dal water and a slice of onion. On good days, a green chilli. She always made me eat first. 'I am not hungry,' she said, and she meant it. Her stomach was full. It was the rest of her that was empty, but none of us knew that yet.
Many women in our chawl were pale like her. Some of the pregnant ones went to hospital and did not come back. People said that is how it is for mill women. Nobody asked why.

Then one day a nurse came up our stairs. She said a lady doctor at the hospital was studying the pale sickness, and wanted to see Aai. My mother did not want to go. I made her go. I held her elbow all the way.

The doctor was called Dr Wills. She was tall and thin, with short grey hair and a plain dress, and she did not talk about the evil eye at all. She talked about food. Through the nurse, she asked my mother what she had eaten yesterday, and the day before, and the day before that. She wrote every answer in a black notebook. Rice. Dal water. Onion. Rice. Tea with sugar. Rice.
'Why does she care what we eat?' I whispered to the nurse. 'My mother is not hungry. She eats every day.'
The nurse asked the doctor. The doctor looked at me for a long moment, as if I had asked a good question.

'Enough food,' she said, and the nurse turned her words into Marathi, 'is not the same as the right food. The rich ladies on Malabar Hill hardly ever get this sickness. They eat rice too. But they also eat milk, vegetables, fruit, eggs and meat. Something is in their plates that is missing from your mother's. Something very small. I am trying to find out what.'

She told us she had fed animals in her laboratory the same food the mill women ate. They became pale too, with the same strange blood. Then she had tried adding different foods, one at a time, to see which one brought them back.
A week later, the nurse came up our stairs again. She was carrying a small brown jar.

Inside was a thick, dark, sticky paste that smelled like salt and burnt bread. It was called Marmite. It was made in England, the nurse said, from the yeast left at the bottom of the big vats where beer is brewed. 'A spoon a day,' she said, 'stirred into warm water or onto rice. The doctor says so.'

The women in our chawl laughed. 'Medicine from beer dregs!' said one. 'English chutney!' said another. Aai made a face like a cat that has tasted lemon. But I had seen the doctor's notebook, and the way she looked at me when I asked my question. So every morning I stirred the brown spoon into warm water, and I stood there until my mother drank it all.

After a week, she could climb two landings without stopping. After two weeks, the inside of her eyelids turned pink. After three, she was laughing at the neighbour's jokes again, and her lips were the colour of lips.

When we went back to the hospital, Dr Wills pricked Aai's finger and put a drop of her blood on a piece of glass. She looked at it through a brass microscope. Then, to my great surprise, she lifted me onto a stool and let me look too.

I saw a crowd of tiny pink circles, packed close like coins in a bag. 'Before,' the nurse explained, 'there were far fewer, and many were too big and strange. Her body could not make good new ones. Now it can.'
'What is in the jar?' I asked. 'What is the medicine?'

The doctor smiled, and the nurse said, 'She says she does not know yet. Something the body needs only a pinch of, but cannot do without. It is in yeast. She thinks it is in other foods too. Leaves, perhaps. Dals. Liver. She will keep looking.'

I thought about our village in the Konkan, before we came to the city. My grandmother used to send me to pick wild leaves after the first rain. Taakla, she called them. We ate them with bhakri. In Bombay, leaves cost money, and there was never enough money for leaves.
My sister was born in March. She was small and loud and perfectly pink, and Aai held her and did not turn the colour of the moon again.

That summer I found a broken kerosene tin and filled it with earth from the railway side. I begged a pinch of methi seeds from the vegetable woman and pushed them in with my finger. I watered them every morning before the mill whistle.
When the first leaves came, small and round and green, I picked a handful. I washed them at the tap, chopped them as fine as I could, and stirred them into my mother's dal.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn is the doctor's sentence, 'Enough food is not the same as the right food.' Sakhu's stomach was full of rice every day, but her diet was not balanced. It was missing a vitamin, later named folate, that the body needs only in tiny amounts to make new blood cells. Kamal's ending joins the two ideas without saying so: the missing thing was in leaves. The story also shows that whether a family eats a balanced diet often depends on money and work, not on knowing better. It quietly credits a woman scientist, a girl who asked the right question, and the women whose illness was taken seriously at last.
ask: Aai said she was not hungry. Why was she still ill?
What did the doctor mean when she said 'enough food is not the same as the right food'?
Why do you think the rich ladies on Malabar Hill did not get the pale sickness?
The doctor said she did not know yet what was in the jar. Was it brave or strange for a doctor to say that?
Why did Kamal grow methi at the end? What did she understand?
Why could Kamal's family not buy leaves in the city? Whose fault was that?

games.title: Cell Delivery

printables.title: 24 food cards to cut out (each shows what it gives the body)
items: Sprouts chaat: 1 protein, 1 vitamin C, 1 fibre
Boiled egg: 2 protein, 1 fat, 1 vitamin A
Til laddoo: 1 energy, 1 calcium, 1 iron, 1 fat
Handful of peanuts: 1 protein, 1 fat, 1 energy
Keerai poriyal (spinach): 1 iron, 1 vitamin A, 1 fibre
Mango: 1 energy, 1 vitamin A, 1 vitamin C

printables.title: My Body sheet: six cells, each with boxes to tick
items: Blood-making cell: needs 1 iron and 1 vitamin C
Eye cell: needs 1 vitamin A and 1 fat
Gut-lining cell: needs 2 fibre (the microbes turn fibre into their food)
Water drop: needs 1 water. Without it, the game ends with no cells fed.

rules: Each player has a My Body sheet. Shuffle the 24 food cards. Lay 5 face up in a row. This row is the market. Put the rest in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take one card from the market. Tick the boxes it fills on your sheet. Then fill the market back up to 5 from the pile.
Extra ticks are not kept. If your Brain cell already has their 2 energy, more energy does not count.
A cell is fed when all their boxes are ticked. Colour them in.
Each player gets 8 turns, like the meals and snacks of one day.

Your body also needs water. Tick the Water drop by taking the buttermilk card, or by using one turn to say 'I drink water' instead of taking a card. If your Water drop is empty at the end, none of your cells count.
With friends or a parent: after 8 turns each, the player with the most fed cells wins. A tie goes to whoever fed the Gut-lining cell.
Playing alone: try to feed all six cells and tick the Water drop within 8 turns. Then try in 7, then in 6. Doing it in 5 is very hard and needs luck.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 food cards. 2. Give each player a My Body sheet and a pencil. 3. Shuffle the cards and lay 5 face up as the market.
flow.say: Your body is made of trillions of cells. Each one needs different things from food. In this game, you are the blood. You carry food to six hungry cells.
flow.kid: You are the blood. Your job is to feed six hungry cells. Each cell needs something different. Lay out 5 food cards as the market.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cell Delivery, a card game about how different foods feed different cells in the body. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Point at the Muscle cell on the sheet and ask which market card would help them.
flow.say: The Muscle cell needs 2 protein. Which card in the market would feed them best?
flow.kid: Look at the Muscle cell. They need 2 protein. Which card gives protein?

check.q: The Muscle cell needs 2 protein. Which card feeds them in one go?
check.why: Moong dal gives 2 protein, so the dal feeds the Muscle cell in one turn. Muscles are built from the amino acids in protein. Rice gives energy, not much protein. Ghee gives fat. Amla gives vitamin C. Picking rice usually means thinking 'filling' food builds muscles. Being full is not the same as getting protein.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. On each turn, take one market card, read it out and tick the boxes it fills. Or use the turn to drink water. 3. Refill the market. 4. Each player has 8 turns.
flow.say: Before you pick, look at which cells are still hungry. A card that gives three different things can be better than one that gives a lot of one thing.
flow.kid: Take turns. Pick one market card. Tick the boxes it fills. Which cells are still hungry?
flow.parent: Good players notice that one-thing cards, like rice, jalebi or ghee, fill only one cell. Mixed cards, like ragi mudde, dal, egg or til laddoo, fill several. The Eye cell is tricky: they need vitamin A and fat. Egg does both at once. Carrot and a spoon of ghee also work, just as carrots cooked in oil give more vitamin A. Don't call jalebi or chips a bad card. They are fine cards that give energy, just not much else.

ask.q: Why is the Gut-lining cell fed by fibre, when we cannot digest fibre?
good: Our gut microbes eat the fibre and make food for the gut cells.
The microbes turn fibre into something the gut lining can use.

flow.do: When someone takes the jalebi or the chips, pause and ask the question below.
flow.say: Jalebi gives 2 energy, which is a lot. Why is it not enough to win on its own?
flow.kid: Someone took the jalebi! It gives 2 energy. Why can't jalebi feed every cell?

ask.q: Why can't one food feed every cell?
good: Jalebi gives energy but no protein, calcium or vitamins.
You need many kinds of food.

flow.do: 1. Count each player's fed cells and find the winner. 2. Look at the winner's cards together.
flow.say: Look at the cards the winner chose. How many different kinds of food did they eat? What does that tell us about a balanced diet?
flow.kid: Count your fed cells. Look at your 8 cards. How many kinds of food did you eat?
flow.think: In the game, extra energy was thrown away. In a real body, what happens to extra energy?

check.q: Which set of cards feeds the most different cells?
options: Moong dal, ragi mudde, amla, boiled egg
check.why: Dal, ragi mudde, amla and egg give protein, energy, calcium, iron, fibre, vitamin C, vitamin A and fat. That feeds all six cells. The first set is all energy foods. The third set is mostly fat. Picking the first set usually means counting how much food there is, not how many kinds.

games.context: This is a card game about why we need many kinds of food. Each player is the blood, carrying food to six cells that each need something different: muscle, brain, bone, blood-making, eye and gut-lining cells.

games.title: What's Missing? (a thali puzzle game)

printables.title: 16 thali cards to cut out (each lists one meal)
items: Chapati, dal, a glass of water
Rice, fish curry, a glass of water
Curd rice, a glass of water
Bread, jam, a glass of milk
Ragi dosa, sambar with drumstick and pumpkin, buttermilk

printables.title: Three colour tokens per player: yellow (go), red (grow), green (glow)
A tally sheet with each player's name

rules: Shuffle the thali cards and put them face down.
One player turns over a card and reads the meal out loud.
Everyone secretly holds up the token for the colour that is most missing: yellow for go foods, red for grow foods or green for glow foods.
Everyone who picked the right colour scores 1 point.
Then each player says one real food from your kitchen that would fill the gap. A food that is really in the kitchen right now scores 1 extra point.
Some cards are already balanced. If you think nothing is missing, hold up all three tokens together. That scores 2 points if you are right.
Playing alone: read each card, put your token on it, then check the answer list. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Give each player three tokens. 3. Shuffle the cards face down.
flow.say: Every card is a real meal people eat. Our job is not to say a meal is bad. Our job is to spot which colour is missing, and find a food to fill the gap.
flow.kid: Each card is a real meal. Find the colour that is missing. Then find a food to fill the gap.
flow.context: This is the first step of What's Missing?, a quick game about balancing a plate. You spot which kind of food a meal is missing, and suggest one to add.

flow.do: Play the card 'Rice, potato curry, papad' together as practice.
flow.say: Rice, potato curry and papad. Rice and potato are both mostly energy. What is missing most?
flow.kid: Rice, potato curry, papad. Which colour is missing most? Hold up your token.

check.q: Rice, potato curry and papad. Which kind of food is missing most?
check.why: Rice and potato are both mostly starch, which is energy. Papad is made from urad dal, but it is a thin crisp, so it gives only a little protein. The meal needs a bowl of dal or curd for protein, and a green poriyal or salad. Picking 'nothing is missing' usually means counting potato as a vegetable. It is one, but in the body it acts mostly like rice.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. Everyone holds up a token. 3. Score points. 4. Each player names a food from your kitchen to fill the gap.
flow.say: Hold up your token. Now tell me a food in our kitchen right now that would fill the gap.
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Hold up the missing colour. Then name a food from your kitchen to add.
flow.parent: Here are the answers. Chapati and dal need green, so add poriyal or salad. Idli and chutney are low in grow and green, so add sambar with vegetables. Poha and tea need grow and green, so add peanuts, peas or a fruit. Rice and fish curry need green. Aloo paratha and pickle need grow and green, so add curd and salad. Bhakri, pitla and onion is fairly balanced, because pitla is made from besan, a pulse. Accept green or all three tokens. Add a green leaf if you can. Curd rice needs green, so add cucumber or a fruit. Rajma rice needs green. Bread, jam and milk need green. Instant noodles need grow and green, so add an egg or peanuts and vegetables. Egg bhurji and chapati need green. Upma and banana need grow, so add peanuts or curd. Ven pongal and ghee need green, so cook vegetables into the pongal. Puri, chole and lassi need green. Ragi dosa, sambar and buttermilk are already balanced, so that card wins all three tokens.

flow.do: Count the points and find the winner. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Most meals were missing the same colour. Which one? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which colour was missing most often?

ask.q: Which colour was missing most often, and why?
good: Green, because vegetables take time to cook.
Green, because people fill up on rice and chapati.

flow.think: Is it easy for every family to add vegetables to every meal? What makes it hard?
