items.p: In the story The Brown Jar, Kamal's mother, Sakhu, ate rice and thin dal every day and always felt full. Yet she grew pale and ill. Why?
opts: Enough food is not the same as the right food. Her meals were missing something her body needed.
Feeling full always means the body is well fed
items.why: Sakhu's stomach was full, but her meals had almost no vegetables, fruit, milk or eggs. So her body was short of a vitamin it needs only a pinch of. A full stomach and a balanced diet are not the same thing.

items.p: Many people use the word 'diet' to mean eating less. What does a balanced diet really mean? Give an example from your own home.
items.a: A balanced diet means eating many kinds of food, in about the right amounts, over a day or a week. It does not mean eating less. For example, in my home we eat idli with sambar in the morning, rice, dal and poriyal at lunch, and fruit in the evening.
items.why: A strong answer says 'many kinds' and 'over a day or a week', and gives a real example from the child's own meals.

items.p: Sort these foods by their main job in your body.
items.why: Ragi and idli are mostly starch, which gives energy. Dal and egg give protein to build the body. Keerai, which is spinach and other greens, and papaya give vitamins, minerals and fibre. Many foods do more than one job, so this is each food's main job.

items.p: Meenakshi says, "Potato is a vegetable. So a plate of rice and potato curry is half vegetables." What is the mistake in her thinking?
opts: Potato is mostly starch, so in the body it acts more like rice than like greens
items.why: Potato grows in the soil like a vegetable, but it is mostly starch, which gives energy. So that plate is nearly all energy food. Greens, beans, carrots or gourds would fill the vegetable half.

items.p: Food is broken into tiny pieces that are small enough to pass into the ____, which carries them to every cell.
items.why: Digestion breaks food into tiny building blocks. These pass through the wall of the gut into the blood. The blood carries them to all your cells.

items.p: Eating one plate of jalebis at a wedding makes your whole diet unhealthy.
items.why: False. A diet is what you usually eat over many days. Sweets on special days are part of a balanced diet. What matters is the everyday pattern.

items.p: Why is it better to eat vegetables of many colours, not the same one every day?
opts: Different vegetables carry different vitamins and minerals, so a mix gives the body more of what it needs
Bright colours make food taste better
One vegetable has every vitamin, so the colour does not matter
items.why: Orange carrots and pumpkin give beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A. Dark green keerai gives iron and folate. Tomatoes and amla give vitamin C. No one vegetable has everything, so a mix fills more gaps.

items.p: Remember the Paper Window Test. Which food left a see-through spot that stayed?
items.why: Peanuts carry fat, which leaves a see-through spot that does not dry. Apple has almost no fat, and water dries away. If you picked water, you may have looked at the paper before the water had time to dry.
items.context: In the Paper Window Test, you rub foods on paper and wait 15 minutes. A see-through spot that stays means fat.

items.p: Before the Paper Window Test, make a guess. Will a piece of fresh coconut leave a see-through spot? Why do you think so? How would the test show whether you were right?
items.a: I think yes, because coconut is oily and we make coconut oil from it. If the spot is still see-through after 15 minutes, that shows fat. If it dries away, my guess was wrong. Fresh coconut is about one third fat, so it does leave a spot.
items.why: A strong answer gives a guess with a reason, then says what result would prove it right or wrong.
items.context: In the Paper Window Test, you rub foods on paper and wait 15 minutes. A see-through spot that stays means fat.

items.p: Match each nutrient to one of its jobs.
pairs: helps mend cuts and take in iron
items.why: Each nutrient has its own jobs. Protein builds the body. Calcium hardens bones. Iron carries oxygen in the blood. Vitamin C helps mend skin and take in iron from plant foods.

items.p: Put the journey of a spoon of dal in order.
items.why: The dal is chewed in the mouth. Acid and enzymes break it down in the stomach. In the small intestine it is cut into tiny pieces called amino acids. These pass into the blood. A muscle cell builds them into their own protein.

items.p: Lakshmi loves dosa and wants to eat only dosa, every meal, every day. Dosa gives energy and some protein. What would her body be short of, and why?
items.a: She would be short of vitamins like vitamin C, minerals like calcium and iron, and fibre, because dosa has very little of these. No single food has every nutrient. So she needs vegetables, fruit, curd or milk too.
items.why: A strong answer names at least two missing nutrients and gives the main idea: no single food has everything.

items.p: Draw a balanced thali. Show the half for vegetables and fruit, and the two quarters.
items.a: A plate with half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein foods like dal or curd, and a glass of water.
items.why: Drawing the plate in parts helps you remember the amounts: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter each for grains and protein.
items.art: An empty round thali outline with a small tumbler outline beside it.

items.p: Write a balanced dinner using food your family often cooks. Label each food go, grow or glow.
items.a: Any meal with all three kinds. For example: rice (go), sambar with toor dal (grow), beans poriyal (glow) and a glass of water.
items.why: A balanced meal has at least one food from each group, with water. Using your own family's food shows you can do it at home.

items.p: Water has no energy in it, so it is not a nutrient.
items.why: False. A nutrient is anything the body needs from food and drink, not only things with energy. Water makes up more than half of your body. Blood, spit and the inside of every cell are mostly water.

items.p: Why do dal and rice make such a good pair?
opts: Each fills the other's gap in amino acids
Rice has no protein at all
items.why: Proteins are built from small pieces called amino acids. Grains are a little low in one of them, and dals are low in another. Eaten over the same day, they give the body the full set. Rice does have some protein, just not the perfect mix.

items.p: Why is a little oil or ghee useful when cooking carrots or keerai?
opts: It helps the body take in vitamin A
items.why: Carrots and keerai have beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A. It dissolves in fat. A little fat in the cooking helps the gut take more of it into the blood.

items.p: Remember the Vanishing Blue test. Amla cleared the blue in 3 drops, and mosambi took 24. About how many times as much vitamin C is in a drop of amla as in a drop of mosambi?
opts: Less, because amla needed fewer drops
items.why: Mosambi needed 24 drops to do the job that 3 drops of amla did. 24 divided by 3 is 8, so each drop of amla holds about eight times as much vitamin C. Picking 'less' reads the test backwards: fewer drops means more vitamin C in each drop.
items.context: In the Vanishing Blue test, vitamin C makes a blue iodine and starch liquid turn clear. You count the drops of juice needed.

items.p: Guess before you test. In the Vanishing Blue test, will a packet fruit drink need more drops than fresh amla juice, or fewer? Why do you think so? What should you read on the packet first?
items.a: I think the packet drink will need many more drops, because it is mostly water and sugar, with little real fruit. Vitamin C also breaks down over time. But I should read the label first, because some drinks have vitamin C added.
items.why: A strong answer gives a guess and a reason, and knows that the label can change the guess.
items.context: In the Vanishing Blue test, vitamin C makes a blue iodine and starch liquid turn clear. You count the drops of juice needed.

items.p: Squeezing lemon on dal helps your body take in the iron from the dal.
items.why: True. Vitamin C in lemon helps the gut take in iron from plant foods like dal and keerai. Iron then helps the blood carry oxygen.

items.p: Remember Balloon Bellies. The sugar balloon grew big and the plain water balloon stayed flat. Why was the plain water bottle in the test?
opts: To show what happens with no food, so we can compare
items.why: The plain water bottle had the same yeast and warm water, but no food. It stayed flat. That shows the gas came from the yeast eating, not from the warmth or the water.
items.context: In Balloon Bellies, you feed yeast sugar, atta or nothing, and balloons on the bottles fill with gas.

items.p: Most of the mass of the food your body burns for energy leaves through your breath, as carbon dioxide.
items.why: True. Your cells burn glucose and fat with oxygen. The carbon from the food leaves as carbon dioxide when you breathe out. Many people guess it leaves in poo or sweat, but scientists showed in 2014 that most leaves through the lungs.

items.p: Gut microbes are only harmful germs.
items.why: False. Most of the trillions of tiny living beings in your gut do no harm. Many eat fibre and make acids that feed the cells of your large intestine. A few kinds can make you ill.

items.p: Which school tiffin is the most balanced?
opts: Ragi dosa, sambar, carrot poriyal and buttermilk
items.why: Ragi dosa gives energy, sambar and buttermilk give protein, and carrot poriyal is a protecting food. Buttermilk also gives water. The other two are mostly energy foods.

items.p: A family in Madurai is arguing about ghee.

views.says: Ghee is good food. We have cooked with it for hundreds of years, and it helps the body take in some vitamins.
Ghee is mostly saturated fat. Eating a lot of it for many years may raise the risk of heart disease, so use a little.
No single food is good or bad. It depends on how much you eat, and what else is on your plate.

items.ask: Whose idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For example, fat helps the body take in vitamin A from carrots. Or, scientists still argue about which fats are best for the heart. It then gives a fair point from another side, and may say that the amount and the whole diet matter.
items.why: This is a real argument. Fat is needed, ghee helps take in some vitamins, and scientists still disagree about how much saturated fat is too much.

items.p: Is each one mostly settled by science, or still argued about?
items: We need vitamin C to stay free of scurvy
Sugar eaten often helps cause tooth decay
Exactly which fats are best for the heart
How much gut microbes change our mood
items.why: Vitamin C and scurvy, and sugar and tooth decay, have been tested for many years. Which fats are best, and how much microbes affect the mind, are still being studied.

items.p: Each of these illnesses happens when the body is missing one nutrient. Match each illness to the nutrient.
pairs: One kind of anaemia in pregnant mothers
items.why: Each illness was found to be caused by missing one nutrient, and cured by eating it. Lucy Wills's work in Bombay led to the discovery of folate.

items.p: How does a sugary drink harm teeth?
opts: Bacteria in the mouth eat the sugar and make acid that eats holes in teeth
Sugar is sharp and scratches teeth
items.why: Bacteria living in your mouth feed on sugar and make acid. The acid slowly dissolves the hard outside of the tooth, making holes. The harm comes from living bacteria, not from the sugar scratching.

items.p: Draw the journey of a chapati from your mouth to a brain cell, in four boxes.
items.a: Mouth (chewing and spit), stomach and small intestine (cut into glucose), blood (carrying glucose), brain cell (burning glucose for energy).
items.why: A strong drawing shows the three big ideas: food is broken down, carried by the blood, and used in a cell.
items.art: Four empty boxes in a row joined by arrows.

items.p: Nila is 9 and growing fast. Her grandmother is 70. They eat the same dal. Why might they need different amounts of food?
items.a: Nila is growing, so her cells need extra protein and minerals to build new bone and muscle. She also runs about a lot and burns more energy for her size. Her grandmother has stopped growing, so she may need less food, but still all the same kinds.
items.why: A strong answer says that growing and moving use extra food, and that both still need many kinds.

items.p: Trillions of tiny living beings called microbes live in your gut. They eat the fibre you cannot digest. People disagree about whether they are part of you.

views.who: Meera, a scientist who studies microbes
views.says: Yes. You cannot stay healthy without them. They feed your gut cells, so you and they are one team.
No. They have their own genes and their own lives, and some kinds can make you ill.
They are like guests in a house. They live in me, but they are not me.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from the science. Then answer back from another side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason from the science, for example that microbes make acids that feed the cells of the large intestine, or that they have their own genes. It then answers back fairly from another view.
items.why: Scientists and thinkers really do argue about this. Each view has evidence, so the strength is in the reasons.

items.p: Lucy Wills was a doctor in Bombay in 1928. She saw that richer women in the city rarely got the pale sickness, but mill women often did. Why was this an important clue?
opts: Both breathed the same city air but ate very different food, so food might be the cause
It showed that rich women were stronger
It proved the sickness was caught from other people
items.why: Rich and poor women lived in the same city, but ate very different food. So diet was the clue. Scientists narrow down causes by looking at what is different between groups. 'Stronger' explains nothing, because it does not say why.

items.p: Lucy Wills fed animals the same food the mill women ate. Then she added one new food at a time. Why one at a time, and not many foods together?
items.a: If she added many foods at once and the animals got better, she would not know which food did it. Adding one at a time means that when they get better, she knows that food was the one. That is a fair test.
items.why: A strong answer says that changing one thing at a time shows which thing caused the change.

items.p: Many people think the fat you eat goes straight onto your body as body fat. What really happens to most of it?
opts: It is broken into small pieces, and cells burn it for energy or use it to build their thin skins
It sticks to the belly as it is
All of it leaves the body unused
items.why: Fat is digested like other food. Its pieces go into the blood. Cells burn some for energy and use some to build the thin skin around every cell. The body stores fat only when it gets more energy than it uses, from any food.

items.p: A scientist wants to test whether a food helps children's teeth. Which test is fair?
opts: Two groups of children, the same in every way except that one group eats the food, checked for months
Ask children if they like the food
Give the food to one child and look at her teeth the next day
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing, and uses enough people and enough time. Two matching groups, followed for months, can show a real difference. One child for one day can show almost nothing. Liking a food tells you nothing about teeth.

items.p: Scientists have proved that eating curd every day makes you live longer.
items.why: False. Ilya Mechnikov suggested this in 1907, but it has not been proved. Curd is a good food, but most of its microbes only pass through the gut, and a long life has many causes.

items.p: The same food can raise one person's blood sugar much more than another person's.
items.why: True. A study in Israel in 2015 measured 800 people and found big differences. Gut microbes seemed to be part of the reason. Scientists are still studying it.

items.p: In 1992, food advice in the United States told people to eat 6 to 11 servings of grain a day. Later it was changed to a plate with more vegetables. What does this show about science?
opts: Advice can change when new evidence comes in
The first advice was always right
items.why: Good science changes its advice when the evidence changes. That is a strength, not a weakness. 'Scientists never know anything' goes too far. Many things about food, like the need for vitamins, are very well tested.

items.p: Why might a family not be able to eat a balanced diet, even if they know what one is? Give two reasons.
items.a: For example: vegetables, dals and milk can cost more than rice. There may be no market nearby. Parents may work long hours with no time to cook. In some homes, women and girls eat last and get less.
items.why: Eating well depends on money, time, distance and fairness, not only on knowing. This is why India gives free cooked lunches in government schools.

items.p: Most of the mass of the food your body burns leaves as carbon dioxide in your breath. Where can that carbon go next?
opts: Into a plant, who uses the carbon to make food
items.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use sunlight to build sugar and starch. So the carbon you breathe out can become part of a plant, and maybe someone's food. Matter is never lost, only moved.

items.p: The energy in your food was first caught from the ____ by plants.
items.why: Plants use sunlight to build sugar and starch. Rice, dal and even milk and eggs carry energy that a plant first caught from the Sun.

items.p: A growing child needs some protein most days, because the body cannot store much of it.
items.why: True. Muscles, skin, blood and hair are always being rebuilt, and children are also growing. The body keeps only a small store of amino acids, so it needs more most days.

items.p: Some adverts say a vitamin tablet can take the place of vegetables. What is missing from that idea?
opts: Vegetables also give fibre for gut microbes, water and many other things a tablet does not
Nothing. A tablet is the same as vegetables
Vegetables have no vitamins in them
items.why: A tablet gives only the few vitamins written on it. Vegetables give fibre, water, minerals and many other things. A tablet can help someone who is short of one vitamin, but it cannot do everything a plate of vegetables does.

items.p: Draw yourself as a crowd: your own cells and your gut microbes. Show what each one gets from your lunch.
items.a: Any drawing that shows cells getting glucose, amino acids and minerals, and microbes getting fibre and giving back food for gut cells.
items.why: This drawing is a model. A strong one shows that one meal feeds many different living beings inside you.
items.art: An empty outline of a child's body with a curved gut drawn inside.

items.p: Chew a piece of plain chapati slowly, and it starts to taste a little sweet. Design a fair test: does chewing for longer make it taste sweeter? What will you change, and what will you keep the same?
items.a: Change only the number of chews, for example 5, 15 and 30. Keep the same chapati, the same size of piece and the same person. Rate the sweetness from 1 to 5 each time, and rinse the mouth with water between tries.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing only. The sweetness comes from an enzyme in spit that cuts starch into sugar, so more chewing should mean more sweetness.

experiments.title: The Paper Window Test: which foods carry fat?
experiments.question: Which of our everyday foods carry fat, and which carry a lot?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which foods will leave a see-through spot on the paper? Which will leave nothing? Write your guess next to each food, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the food. Use the same paper, squares of the same size, a piece of food about the size of your thumbnail, and rub each one for the same time, 10 rubs. Oil and water are tested too, so you can see what a fat spot and a water spot look like.
results_table: My guess: fat or no fat?
Spot after 15 minutes: none, small, medium or big

materials.item: a brown paper bag, or a sheet of plain white paper, cut into 8 squares about as big as your palm
pieces of food about the size of your thumbnail: a peanut, a piece of fresh or dry coconut, a cube of paneer, a potato chip or some namkeen, a piece of plain chapati with no ghee, a slice of apple
2 drops of cooking oil and 2 drops of water, to compare
a pencil, a spoon, a steel tumbler of water and a window or a torch

experiments.safety: Only small pieces are used. Wash your hands afterwards. You can eat the leftover food, but not the pieces that were rubbed on paper.

schedule.what: Guess, rub each food on its own square, wait 15 minutes, then hold each square up to the light and record the spots.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each food, as tall as its spot: 0 for none, 1 for small, 2 for medium, 3 for big.

flow.do: 1. Write one food name on each paper square in pencil. 2. Show your child the foods. 3. Ask them to guess which will leave a fat spot, and write the guess.
flow.say: Fat leaves a see-through spot on paper, like a little window. Which of these foods do you think carry fat?
flow.kid: Fat makes paper see-through, like a little window. Which foods carry fat? Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why did you guess that one?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Window Test. You rub foods on paper to find which ones carry fat. Fat is a nutrient the body needs.

flow.do: 1. Rub each food on its own square, 10 firm rubs. 2. Squash the peanut and coconut with the back of a spoon first. 3. Put 2 drops of oil on the oil square and 2 drops of water on the water square.
flow.say: Rub each food firmly, ten times, on its own square. Same rubs for each, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Rub each food on its own square. Count ten rubs. Put oil and water on the last two squares.
flow.parent: Use chapati made without ghee, or the test will find the ghee. Squash hard foods so that their insides touch the paper.

flow.do: 1. Leave the squares flat for 15 minutes so the water can dry. 2. Meanwhile, put 2 drops of oil into a tumbler of water and look from the top. 3. Read the card on why the body needs fat. 4. After 15 minutes, hold each square up to a window or a torch.
flow.say: Water dries away. Fat does not. After 15 minutes, any spot still see-through is fat. Let's look.
flow.kid: Wait 15 minutes. Meanwhile, drop 2 drops of oil into a tumbler of water. Does it mix? Then hold each square up to the light.
flow.parent: Expect big spots from oil, peanut and coconut, and medium ones from paneer and chips. Plain chapati and apple usually leave nothing once dry. If a spot still looks wet, wait 10 minutes more, because water spots can take time to dry. If the paper is very thin, use two layers. The oil in the tumbler floats as round drops and does not mix, even if you stir. Apple can leave a faint sticky mark from its sugar, but a fat spot is much clearer.

chart.title: Made-up example: how big was each see-through spot after 15 minutes?
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your results will be different.

check.q: The water spot dried and disappeared. The oil spot stayed see-through. What does a spot that stays tell you?
check.why: Water dries into the air, so its spot disappears. Fat does not dry, so its window stays. A spot that is still there after 15 minutes means fat. Picking 'water' usually means looking too soon, before the water has dried.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why it matters.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why does the body need foods like these?
flow.kid: Now say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it matters.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: peanuts, coconut and paneer carry fat, and apple and plain chapati carry almost none. What I saw: big see-through spots for peanut and coconut, and no spot for apple. Why: fat builds the thin skin around every cell and helps us take in vitamin A from carrots and palak. So a little fat is part of a balanced diet. Do not let the talk turn into 'fat is bad'. Peanuts and coconut are nourishing foods.

experiments.context: In this experiment you rub foods on paper. Foods with fat leave a see-through spot that stays, like a window. It shows which everyday foods carry fat, a nutrient the body needs in small amounts.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your results will be different.

experiments.title: The Vanishing Blue: which fruit has the most vitamin C?
experiments.question: Which juice has the most vitamin C: amla, guava, lemon, mosambi or a packet fruit drink?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Put the juices in order, from the most vitamin C to the least. Write your order down, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the juice. Each bowl gets the same amount of blue liquid, 2 tablespoons. Use the same dropper or straw for every juice, rinsed in between. Swirl the same way after each drop, and stop at the same point: when the blue has gone. Water is tested too, to show that just adding liquid does not clear the blue.
results_table: Drops needed to clear the blue

materials.item: half a cup of rice water: the cloudy water poured off when cooking rice, cooled. Or 1 pinch of cornflour boiled in half a cup of water by a grown-up, then cooled
povidone-iodine antiseptic liquid, the brown antiseptic in many medicine boxes and at any chemist, or tincture of iodine
6 small steel bowls or glasses, and a tablespoon
a plastic dropper, or a drinking straw (dip it in, put your thumb on top, and lift)
juices, about 1 tablespoon each: amla (grate one or two and squeeze through a cloth), guava (mash and squeeze), lemon, mosambi or orange, a packet fruit drink, and plain water
a white paper or plate to put under the bowls, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the iodine. It stains skin and clothes, and it must never be swallowed. Nobody drinks anything from the test bowls. Pour them down the sink afterwards and wash the bowls.

schedule.what: Make the blue test liquid, squeeze the juices, then count drops of each juice until the blue disappears.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each juice, as tall as the number of drops. The shortest bar has the most vitamin C.

flow.do: 1. Show the fruits and the packet drink. 2. Ask your child to guess the order, from most vitamin C to least. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Vitamin C helps mend cuts, keeps gums strong and helps your body take in iron. Which of these juices do you think has the most?
flow.kid: Vitamin C helps your body mend cuts and take in iron. Which juice has the most? Guess the order.

ask.q: Why did you guess that order?
good: Lemons are sour, so they must have a lot.
The packet says it has vitamins.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Vanishing Blue test. You use a blue liquid made with iodine and starch. Vitamin C makes the blue disappear, so you can count which juice has the most.

flow.do: 1. In a jug, mix 1 cup of water with 2 tablespoons of rice water. 2. Add iodine drop by drop and stir. About 5 to 10 drops makes it the dark blue of fountain-pen ink. 3. Pour 2 tablespoons into each of the 6 bowls. 4. Put the bowls on a white paper.
flow.say: Iodine turns starch dark blue. Vitamin C undoes that and makes the blue disappear. The more vitamin C a juice has, the fewer drops it needs.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes rice water and iodine. It turns dark blue. Pour the same amount into six bowls.
flow.parent: The starch in rice water turns iodine blue-black. If the liquid is almost black, add more water until you can see through it a little. If it stays brown, add a little more rice water. A very dark start makes every juice need many more drops.

flow.do: 1. Add amla juice to the first bowl, one drop at a time. 2. Swirl after every drop and count. 3. Stop when the blue has gone, and write the number. 4. Rinse the dropper. 5. Do the same for each juice, and for water.
flow.say: One drop, swirl, look. One drop, swirl, look. Stop the moment the blue is gone.
flow.kid: Add one drop. Swirl. Look. Count each drop. Stop when the blue is gone.
flow.parent: Amla usually clears the blue in just a few drops. Guava is usually next. Lemon and mosambi need many more drops, often about the same number. Packet drinks often need many drops, unless vitamin C has been added, which is a real result too. Read the packet to check. Water never clears it. Stop any juice at 40 drops and write '40 or more'. Orange-coloured juices tint the liquid, so look for the blue going, not for it turning clear. Amla also has other substances, called tannins, that clear the blue too. So the test measures vitamin C together with some similar substances, not vitamin C alone.

chart.title: Made-up example: drops of juice needed to clear the blue
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Fewer drops means more vitamin C. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: Amla cleared the blue in 3 drops. Lemon needed 18 drops. Which has more vitamin C?
check.why: Fewer drops means more vitamin C in each drop. Amla needed only 3, so each drop of amla has much more vitamin C than a drop of lemon. Picking lemon usually means thinking 'more drops, more vitamin C'. It is the other way round, like needing fewer big coins than small coins to make ten rupees.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think amla is so good at this?
flow.kid: Now say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: amla has the most vitamin C, and the packet drink had very little. What I saw: amla cleared the blue in 3 drops, lemon in 18, and the packet drink was still blue at 40. Why: vitamin C reacts with the iodine and takes away its blue. So the fewer drops, the more vitamin C. Extra: vitamin C is also lost when food is boiled a long time or cut and left open. Try a squeezed lemon juice left out overnight, if you are curious. The change may be small.

flow.do: Talk about the iron partners. Squeeze lemon on a bowl of dal at the next meal, or eat a guava with your lunch.
flow.say: Vitamin C has another job. It helps your body take in the iron from dal, palak and bajra. So the old habit of squeezing lemon on dal also helps your body.
flow.kid: Vitamin C helps your body take iron from dal. Squeeze lemon on your dal at dinner.
flow.think: Old recipes put lemon on dal and amla in chutney, long before anyone knew about vitamins. Why do you think these habits lasted?

experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a blue liquid with rice water and iodine. Vitamin C makes the blue disappear. By counting drops, you find which juice has the most vitamin C.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Fewer drops means more vitamin C. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: Balloon Bellies: what do microbes like to eat?
experiments.question: Do tiny living things make more gas when they are fed sugar, flour or nothing at all?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which balloon will grow biggest: the sugar bottle, the atta bottle or the plain water bottle? Will any stay flat? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the food. Every bottle gets the same yeast, 2 teaspoons, the same warm water, 150 millilitres, and sits in the same place for the same time. The plain water bottle has no food, so you can see what happens without any.

materials.item: 3 empty plastic bottles of the same size, 200 to 500 millilitres
3 balloons, stretched a few times first so they blow up easily
6 teaspoons of dry baking yeast, about 20 grams (instant yeast, sold in small packets or jars)
1 tablespoon of sugar and 1 tablespoon of atta
warm water, as warm as a comfortable bath, not hot, and a measuring cup
a funnel or a paper cone, a marker, a piece of string and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up mixes the warm water so it is never hot. Don't drink the mixture. When you finish, take the balloons off outside or over a sink, because the gas smells of yeast.

schedule.what: Set up three bottles of yeast with sugar, atta or nothing. Measure the balloons every 15 minutes for 45 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each bottle, as tall as its balloon was round after 45 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the yeast. 2. Explain that each grain is a clump of tiny living fungi, resting until they get water, warmth and food. 3. Ask them to guess which food the yeast will like best.
flow.say: Yeast is a living thing, a tiny fungus. Each grain holds thousands of them, resting. When they eat, they make a gas. Your gut microbes do the same thing with the fibre you cannot digest. Which food will these ones like best?
flow.kid: Yeast is alive. They are a tiny fungus, resting. When they eat, they make gas. Which food will it like best?
flow.context: This is the first step of Balloon Bellies. You feed yeast, a tiny living fungus, three different foods and watch balloons fill with the gas they make. It is a model of how gut microbes eat.

flow.do: 1. Label the bottles Sugar, Atta and Water. 2. Using a funnel, put 2 teaspoons of yeast in each. 3. Add 1 tablespoon of sugar to the first and 1 tablespoon of atta to the second. Add nothing to the third. 4. Pour 150 millilitres of warm water into each. 5. Swirl gently. 6. Stretch a balloon over each mouth.
flow.say: Same yeast, same warm water, same bottles. Only the food is different. That is what makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Put yeast in all three bottles. Add sugar to one and atta to one. Add warm water. Put on the balloons.
flow.parent: Test the water on the inside of your wrist. It should feel warm but not hot. Hot water kills yeast, and cold water keeps them resting. Stretch each balloon a few times first so it fills more easily.

flow.do: 1. Put the bottles in a warm spot, out of the fan. 2. Every 15 minutes, wrap a string round the fattest part of each balloon, then measure the string on a ruler. 3. Write the numbers. 4. In between, play Cell Delivery or read the story.
flow.say: Let's measure each balloon with the string. Which one is growing fastest?
flow.kid: Every 15 minutes, measure each balloon with a string. Write down the numbers.
flow.parent: The sugar balloon usually starts to stand up within 15 to 20 minutes, and fills more by 45. The atta balloon grows slowly, because enzymes in the flour must first cut its starch into sugar for the yeast. The water balloon stays almost flat. If the balloons are still small at 45 minutes, keep going to 60 minutes. Sometimes nothing happens at all after 20 minutes. Then the water was too hot or too cold, or the yeast was old. Test the yeast: a spoonful in warm sugar water should froth within 10 minutes. In cold months, stand the bottles in a bowl of warm water.

chart.title: Made-up example: how round each balloon was after 45 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Measure round the fattest part of each balloon with a string, then hold the string against a ruler.

check.q: The sugar balloon grew big. The water balloon stayed flat. What does that show?
options: Yeast makes gas only when they have food to eat
Balloons grow by themselves in warm places
Sugar makes gas without the yeast
check.why: Every bottle had the same yeast and the same warm water. Only the food was different. So the gas came from the yeast eating the food. Picking 'balloons grow by themselves' misses the water bottle, which was warm too and stayed flat. To check the last idea, you could try sugar and warm water with no yeast.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why. Then talk about how the yeast is like, and unlike, gut microbes.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why? Now, your gut microbes are not yeast. They are mostly bacteria. But they also eat and make gas. What do they eat?
flow.kid: Now say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. What do your gut microbes eat?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: yeast makes gas when they eat, and they like sugar best. What I saw: the sugar balloon was 28 centimetres round after 45 minutes, atta 13 and water about 1. Why: the yeast ate the food and gave off carbon dioxide gas. Our gut microbes eat fibre from dal, poriyal and fruit. They also make gas, and acids that feed our gut cells. A model is never exactly the real thing. Yeast is a fungus, and most gut microbes are bacteria.

experiments.context: In this experiment you feed yeast, a tiny living fungus, three different foods. Balloons on the bottles fill with the gas the yeast makes as they eat. It is a model of the trillions of microbes in your gut, which eat the fibre you cannot digest.

activities.title: Yesterday's Plate: a colour sort

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
crayons or pens in four colours: yellow, red, green and blue

activities.safety: None. This is a looking and thinking activity.

schedule.what: List everything you ate and drank yesterday, mark each food with its colours, and notice the pattern.

activities.record: Your list of yesterday's food, with coloured dots beside each one, and one sentence about what you noticed.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to tell you everything they ate and drank yesterday, from waking up to bedtime. 2. Write it as a list, one food per line. 3. Include drinks, snacks and anything nibbled.
flow.say: Let's be food detectives. Tell me everything you ate and drank yesterday. Start from the moment you woke up.
flow.kid: What did you eat and drink yesterday? Start from when you woke up. Write one food on each line.
flow.parent: Include water, milk, tea, biscuits and fruit. Children often forget snacks and drinks. Do not comment on any food. This is noticing, not marking.
flow.context: This is the first step of Yesterday's Plate. You list your food from yesterday and sort it by the job each food does in your body.

flow.do: Help your child put coloured dots next to each food. Yellow for energy foods (go). Red for body-building foods (grow). Green for vegetables and fruits (glow). Blue for water and drinks. Some foods get two dots.
flow.say: Yellow is for go foods that give energy, like rice and chapati. Red is for grow foods that build your body, like dal, milk and eggs. Green is for glow foods, the vegetables and fruits. Blue is for water.
flow.kid: Yellow dot for energy foods. Red dot for body-building foods. Green dot for vegetables and fruits. Blue dot for drinks.

check.q: Which colour dot does a bowl of dal get?
check.why: Dal is full of protein, which builds and mends the body, so it gets a red dot. Dal also has some energy and fibre, so a yellow dot as well is fine. Picking blue usually means thinking of thin dal as a drink. It is watery, but its main job is protein.

flow.parent: Tricky ones: milk is red and blue. Potato is yellow. Poha with peanuts and peas is yellow, red and green. Sugar in tea is yellow. Ghee and oil can be yellow, since fat gives energy.

flow.do: 1. Count the dots of each colour. 2. Ask: what do you notice, and what do you wonder? 3. Write one sentence of each.
flow.say: Count each colour. What do you notice? Is there a colour with lots of dots, or one with very few? What do you wonder about that?
flow.kid: Count each colour. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Say one of each.

ask.q: What do you notice about your colours?

good: Why do I need green foods?
Is it bad to have lots of yellow?
What happens to the food after I eat it?

flow.parent: Most children find lots of yellow and few greens. That is common and nothing to worry about. Keep their wonder questions. The rest of the unit answers them.
flow.think: Your body is made of trillions of cells. Do you think they all need the same thing from food?

activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You list what you ate yesterday and give each food a colour for the job it does. Then you look for a pattern, without judging.

setup.caption: 2. Give each food its colour dots.

activities.title: Build a Balanced Thali

materials.item: a plate or thali and a few small bowls (katoris)
the food your family has cooked for lunch or dinner today
some quick extras if a colour is missing: a cucumber, a tomato, a banana, a handful of peanuts, a lemon, a bowl of curd

activities.safety: A grown-up serves hot food. The child serves cool foods and plans the plate.

schedule.what: Plan and serve your own balanced plate from today's food, check it has every colour, and fill any gap.

activities.record: A drawing or photo of your plate, labelled go, grow and glow, and one sentence on what you added.

flow.do: 1. Look together at what has been cooked today. 2. Ask your child to name each dish and give it a colour: yellow (go), red (grow) or green (glow).
flow.say: Let's look at what we have today. For each dish, tell me its colour. Is it a go, a grow or a glow food?
flow.kid: Look at today's food. Is each dish go, grow or glow?
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Balanced Thali. You plan and serve your own plate from today's food, so that it has every kind of food your body needs.

flow.do: Show your child the plate. Explain the three parts with your finger: half the plate, a quarter and a quarter.
flow.say: Scientists at India's National Institute of Nutrition suggest a plate that is about half vegetables and fruits. One quarter is grains or millets. One quarter is dal, curd, egg, paneer, fish or meat. We drink water with it.
flow.kid: Half your plate is vegetables and fruit. A quarter is rice or chapati. A quarter is dal, curd, egg or paneer. Add water.

check.q: On a balanced plate, which part is the biggest?
check.why: About half the plate is vegetables and fruit. They give many vitamins, minerals and fibre, but not much energy, so we need a lot of them. Picking rice or chapati is natural, because most Indian plates are piled with rice or chapati. They give energy, and a quarter of the plate is usually enough.

flow.do: 1. Your child serves the cool foods into the right parts. 2. You serve the hot foods where your child points. 3. Put dal and curd in katoris if that is easier.
flow.say: You plan it and I'll help with the hot things. Where should the poriyal go? Where should the rice go?
flow.kid: You plan the plate. A grown-up serves the hot food. Point to where each dish goes.
flow.parent: One-pot meals count too. Pongal and khichdi are grain and dal together. Biryani is grain with meat or vegetables. Then just add a raita or salad. Don't worry about exact amounts. Half and quarters are a guide, not a rule.

flow.do: Look at the plate together. Ask: is any colour missing? If so, find a quick fix in the kitchen.
flow.say: Is any colour missing? What could we add in two minutes, with no cooking?
flow.kid: Is any colour missing? Find a quick food to add. No cooking needed.

ask.q: What could we add if green is missing?
What could we add if red is missing?

flow.parent: If nothing is missing, praise the cook. Do not call any family dish wrong. The aim is to notice and add, never to remove or shame.

flow.do: 1. Eat the meal. 2. Afterwards, ask your child to say three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why.
flow.say: After we eat, tell me three things. What do you think about our plate? What was on it? Why does the body need all three colours?
flow.kid: After eating, say three things. What I think. What I saw on my plate. Why my body needs every colour.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: our lunch was balanced. What I saw: bhindi and salad for green, rice for yellow, dal and curd for red, and water. Why: energy foods give fuel, grow foods build my body, and glow foods help everything work. Balance over the whole day matters more than any one plate.

activities.context: This is the main hands-on activity of the unit. You plan and serve your own balanced plate, using the food your family has cooked today.

setup.caption: 1. Imagine your plate in three parts: one half and two quarters.

setup.art: A child spooning poriyal and salad into the big half of a thali, a grown-up placing hot rice in one quarter.
setup.caption: 2. Fill half with vegetables, a quarter with grains, a quarter with dal or curd.

activities.title: The Paper-Clip Journey: from chapati to cell

materials.item: about 30 paper clips, ideally in three colours (or strips of coloured paper made into a paper chain)
a piece of thin card, like a cereal box, with a slot cut in it just wide enough for one paper clip
a small ball of wool or cotton thread, for fibre
three small boxes or bowls labelled Muscle cell, Brain cell and Gut microbes

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the slot in the card with scissors.

schedule.what: Use paper-clip chains to act out how food is cut into building blocks, passes into the blood and is rebuilt in your cells.

activities.record: Draw the journey in four pictures: the chain, the cutting, the slot, the cells.

flow.do: 1. Make one long chain of 10 clips of the same colour. This is starch from chapati. 2. Make a chain of 12 clips in mixed colours. This is protein from dal.
flow.say: Starch is a long chain of glucose, all the same kind of piece. Protein is a chain of amino acids, in many kinds. Here they are as paper clips.
flow.kid: Make a long chain of same-colour clips. That is starch from chapati. Make a mixed-colour chain. That is protein from dal.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper-Clip Journey. Paper-clip chains stand for food. You find out why food must be cut into tiny pieces before your body can use it.

flow.do: Stand the card up. Ask your child to hold a whole chain bunched up in one hand and push the bunch through the slot. It will not fit.
flow.say: This card is the wall of your small intestine. On the other side is your blood. Can the whole chain get through?
flow.kid: The card is your gut wall. Blood is on the other side. Try to push a whole chain through the slot.

check.q: Why won't the whole chain fit through the gut wall?
options: It is too big. It must be cut into single pieces first.
check.why: The gut wall lets through only very small pieces, like single glucose or amino acids. Big chains like starch and protein must first be cut up. That cutting is digestion. Picking 'the gut wall is closed' misses that tiny pieces do get through, all the time.

flow.parent: If your child threads the chain through one clip at a time, say that this is like cutting it: the real gut wall takes in only single pieces, one at a time, never a whole chain.

flow.do: 1. Your child is now the enzymes. They unhook the clips one at a time. 2. Push each single clip through the slot into the 'blood' side. 3. Try to unhook the ball of wool. It cannot be cut up.
flow.say: You are the enzymes now, the tiny scissors in your spit and gut. Unhook each clip and send it through. Now try the fibre.
flow.kid: You are the enzymes. Unhook the clips one by one. Push each one through. Now try to cut the wool.
flow.parent: The ball of wool is fibre. Our enzymes cannot cut it, so it cannot pass through the wall. It travels on to the large intestine, where the gut microbes eat it. Put it in the Gut microbes bowl.

flow.do: 1. On the blood side, take the single clips to the cell bowls. 2. In the Muscle cell bowl, join the mixed clips into a new chain in a new order. 3. Put the same-colour clips in the Brain cell bowl, where they are burned for energy.
flow.say: Your muscle cells take the amino acids and join them in a new order, to make your own muscle protein. Your brain cells burn the glucose for energy.
flow.kid: Take the clips to the cells. Join the mixed clips in a new order. That is new muscle. Put the plain clips in the brain bowl.

check.q: The protein from dal is cut up and rebuilt in your muscle. Whose protein is it now?
check.why: The amino acids are joined in a new order made by your own cells. So the new protein is yours. This is how food becomes you. Picking 'the dal's' is a good thought, since the pieces came from dal. But the new chain has a different order and a different job.

flow.think: Your muscle is built from dal, and the dal plant was built from air, water, soil and sunlight. So where does the dal end and you begin?

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the journey in four pictures.
flow.say: Draw the four steps: the chain, the cutting, the slot and the cells.
flow.kid: Draw four pictures: the chain, the cutting, the slot and the cells.

activities.context: This is a model activity. Paper-clip chains stand for food. You cut them into single building blocks, pass them through the gut wall and build them into new things, as your body does with food.

setup.art: A long chain of silver paper clips labelled 'starch from chapati' and a chain of mixed coloured clips labelled 'protein from dal', on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Make a long chain for starch and a mixed chain for protein.

setup.art: A child's hands unhooking paper clips one by one, labelled 'enzymes cutting'.
setup.caption: 2. Be the enzymes. Unhook the clips one at a time.

setup.art: A piece of card standing up with a narrow slot, single paper clips passing through it into a bowl labelled 'blood', while a whole chain is stuck at the slot.
setup.caption: 3. Push them through the gut wall slot. Only single clips fit.

activities.title: How Many Spoons? Reading a packet label

materials.item: 2 to 4 packets or bottles from home or a shop: a juice box, a flavoured milk, a soft drink, a glucose biscuit packet
a teaspoon, a small bowl of sugar and a saucer for each packet
a whole orange, mosambi or banana to compare
a pencil and paper

activities.safety: None. Pour the sugar back into the jar afterwards, so it is not wasted.

schedule.what: Find the sugar on drink labels, turn the grams into teaspoons, and spoon out that much sugar to see it.

activities.record: A table with each packet, its grams of sugar, and its teaspoons, plus a photo or drawing of the saucers.

flow.do: 1. Find the Nutrition Information box on each packet. 2. Find the line 'Sugars' or 'Total sugars'. 3. Check whether the number is for 100 millilitres or for the whole pack.
flow.say: Most food packets in India have a small table called Nutrition Information. Let's find the line that says sugars.
flow.kid: Find the Nutrition Information box. Find the word 'Sugars'. Read the number.
flow.parent: Many labels give sugar per 100 millilitres or per 100 grams. If the pack is 200 millilitres, double the number. Some labels also show 'added sugars', which is sugar put in during making.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Many Spoons? You read the sugar on drink and snack labels, then spoon out that much sugar to see it.

flow.do: Help your child divide the grams of sugar in the whole pack by 4. A level teaspoon of sugar weighs about 4 grams.
flow.say: One level teaspoon of sugar weighs about 4 grams. So we divide the grams by 4 to get teaspoons.
flow.kid: One teaspoon of sugar is about 4 grams. Divide the grams by 4.

check.q: A juice box has 24 grams of sugar. One teaspoon is about 4 grams. How many teaspoons is that?
check.why: 24 divided by 4 is 6. So the juice box holds about 6 teaspoons of sugar. Picking 24 means forgetting to divide. Picking 4 mixes up the grams in one spoon with the number of spoons.

flow.do: 1. Spoon that many level teaspoons of sugar onto a saucer in front of each packet. 2. Put the whole fruit at the end.
flow.say: Let's see what that sugar looks like. Count the spoons out loud as you go.
flow.kid: Spoon out the sugar for each packet. Count out loud. Put the fruit at the end.
flow.parent: Fruit has natural sugar too. But it is locked inside fibre and water, so it reaches the blood slowly. And few people eat four oranges at once. The World Health Organization advises keeping added sugar under a tenth of our food energy, and lower is better. For a child, a tenth is roughly 10 teaspoons in a whole day, and half of that is even better. These are sometimes drinks, not forbidden ones.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw. Then pour the sugar back into the jar.
flow.say: What surprised you? Which drink would you choose on a hot afternoon, and which on a birthday?
flow.kid: Which saucer surprised you? What would you drink on a hot day? What on a birthday?

ask.q: What could we drink instead on an ordinary hot day?

flow.think: Why do you think sugary drinks have such bright packets and adverts?

activities.context: This is a label-reading activity. You find how much sugar is in some drinks and snacks, then spoon that much sugar onto saucers so you can see it.

activities.title: Grandmother's Plate: an interview

materials.item: a grandparent or older person to talk to, in person or on the phone
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Ask an elder what they ate as a child, and compare their plate with yours.

activities.record: A drawing of the elder's childhood plate next to your own, with three differences written underneath.

flow.do: Help your child ask these questions and write down the answers. What did you eat for breakfast when you were my age? What grains did you eat? Which vegetables and leaves? Where did your food come from? Did you have sweets, and when? Who cooked, and who ate first?
flow.say: Let's be food historians. We'll ask Paati, Aaji or Nani what she ate when she was your age. Real scientists collect old knowledge like this.
flow.kid: Ask your grandparent what they ate when they were your age. Write down their answers.
flow.parent: Many elders will mention millets like ragi, bajra or jowar, wild or seasonal leaves, and fewer packet foods. Some will mention hunger or hard times. Listen with respect. The question 'who ate first?' often shows that women and girls ate last and least. That is worth talking about gently.
flow.context: This is the first step of Grandmother's Plate. You interview an elder about what they ate as a child.

flow.do: Draw two plates side by side: the elder's childhood plate and your plate from yesterday.
flow.say: Let's draw both plates. What is the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Draw their plate and your plate side by side. What is the same? What is different?

ask.q: Why do you think people stopped eating millets so much?
good: Shops sell more rice and wheat.

flow.do: Talk about what you have both learned. Ask your elder which of their old foods they miss.
flow.say: Which of their old foods would you like to try? Could we cook one this week?
flow.kid: Which old food would you like to try? Ask if you can cook it together.
flow.think: India asked the United Nations to name 2023 the International Year of Millets. Why might old grains be important for the future?

activities.context: This is an interview activity. You ask a grandparent or another elder what they ate when they were your age, and compare it with your plate today.

activities.title: Hungry or Full? Listening to your body

materials.item: a paper with a scale of five faces drawn on it, from 1 (very hungry) to 5 (very full)
a pencil

activities.safety: None. There is no right or wrong number.

schedule.what: Rate how hungry you are before a meal and how full you are after, and notice what your body tells you.

activities.record: Your two numbers, before and after the meal, and one sentence on what you noticed.

flow.do: Before a meal, show your child the five-face scale. Ask them to point to how hungry they feel right now.
flow.say: Your body tells you when it needs food, and when it has had enough. Point to how hungry you feel now. 1 is very hungry, 5 is very full.
flow.kid: Before you eat, point to how hungry you feel. 1 is very hungry. 5 is very full.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hungry or Full? You notice the signals your body sends about hunger and fullness, before and after a meal.

flow.do: During the meal, halfway through, ask your child to pause, take a breath and check the scale again.
flow.say: Let's stop halfway and check. Has the number changed? The 'I am full' message from your stomach takes a while to reach your brain.
flow.kid: Stop halfway. Take a breath. Has your number changed?
flow.parent: Never use this to make a child eat less or more. Children's hunger changes a lot from day to day, especially when they are growing. The aim is just to notice.

flow.do: After the meal, ask your child to point again, and say what they noticed.
flow.say: How full do you feel now? How did your body tell you?
flow.kid: Point to how full you feel now. How did your body tell you?

ask.q: How does your body tell you it is full?

flow.think: Who in your home eats first, and who eats last? Does everyone get to stop when they are full, and eat when they are hungry?

activities.context: This is a short activity about listening to your own body. Before and after a meal, you mark how hungry or full you feel on a scale of 1 to 5.

projects.title: The 30-Plant Week: feed your gut microbes

materials.item: a big sheet of paper with a table of 7 days, and space for a pictograph
a pencil and green crayon

projects.safety: None. Eat only foods your family normally eats. This is counting, not a challenge to eat strange things.

schedule.what: Write down every different plant you ate today. Grains, dals, vegetables, fruits, nuts, seeds and spices all count.
Add today's new plants. A plant counts only once in the week.
Add today's new plants. Ask the cook which spices went into the dal.
Add today's new plants. Try one plant you have not eaten this week, if your family has one.
Add today's plants, count the week's total, and draw a pictograph of the new plants each day.

projects.record: The week's plant list, the total, and a pictograph where one leaf stands for 2 new plants.
projects.context: In this seven-day project, you count how many different kinds of plants you eat in a week. A large study in 2018 found that people who ate 30 or more kinds of plant a week had more kinds of gut microbes. You end by drawing a pictograph.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with 7 rows, one for each day. 2. After dinner on day 1, list every different plant your child ate. 3. Remember the hidden ones: rice, wheat, the dal, onion, tomato, ginger, jeera, haldi and coriander.
flow.say: Your gut microbes come in hundreds of kinds. Different kinds like different plants. Let's count how many plant kinds you eat this week.
flow.kid: Every kind of plant feeds different gut microbes. Write every plant you ate today. Spices count too.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 30-Plant Week. You count every kind of plant you eat in a week, because different gut microbes eat different plants.

flow.do: Each day for days 2 to 6, add only the plants not already on the list. Write the number of new plants for each day.
flow.say: A plant counts only once in the week. Is there anything new on your plate today?
flow.kid: Each day, add the new plants only. Write how many new ones you found.
flow.wait: Do this for 5 more days, after dinner.
flow.parent: Most families reach 20 to 35 without trying, thanks to Indian spices and dals. Count each dal separately: moong, masoor and toor are different plants. Tea and coffee count. This is not a contest between families. Cheap foods count as much as costly ones. A pinch of ajwain is a plant.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, count the total. 2. Draw a pictograph. One leaf stands for 2 new plants. Half a leaf stands for 1. 3. Look for the day with the most new plants.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a pictograph. One leaf means two new plants. Which day had the most?
flow.kid: Count your total. Draw one leaf for every 2 new plants. Draw half a leaf for 1.

check.q: On Monday you ate 9 new plants. One leaf stands for 2 plants. How many leaves do you draw?
check.why: 9 divided by 2 is 4, with 1 left over. So draw 4 whole leaves and half a leaf for the extra plant. Picking 9 leaves means forgetting that each leaf stands for 2. Picking 2 leaves means using the key the wrong way.

flow.think: Did you reach 30? Your gut microbes are living things with their own lives. What would a week look like from their side?

challenges.title: The Tiffin Week Challenge
challenges.problem: Plan five school tiffins for one week. Each one must be balanced, with go, grow and glow foods. It must survive until lunch without a fridge, and not get soggy. You must be able to help make it in 15 minutes in the morning.
constraints: No fridge between morning and lunch, and Indian summer heat.
Your family's usual budget, with no special shopping.
Made in 15 minutes, with you helping.
Something you will happily eat. No point in a tiffin that comes home full.
materials: a look in your kitchen and your family's weekly shopping list
general: Idli or dosa with a dry chutney powder and a fruit.
Chapati rolled with paneer or egg bhurji and vegetables.

opts: Many kinds of food, in about the right amounts, over a day or week
quiz.why: A balanced diet mixes many kinds of food so the body gets all it needs. It does not mean eating less or only one kind. Picking 'eating less' mixes up 'diet' with going on a diet.

quiz.p: Which group is dal, egg and paneer in?
quiz.why: Dal, eggs and paneer are full of protein, which builds and mends the body. Picking glow might mean thinking all healthy foods are protecting foods.

quiz.p: Moong dal gives protein, iron and fibre. What does this show?
opts: Many foods do more than one job
Iron is a kind of protein
quiz.why: Most foods give several nutrients. The food groups are a helpful map, not strict boxes. Picking 'iron is a kind of protein' mixes up a mineral and a nutrient that builds the body.

quiz.p: On a balanced plate, about how much is vegetables and fruit?
quiz.why: About half. Vegetables and fruit give vitamins, minerals and fibre, but little energy, so we need a lot of them. Picking a quarter is close to what many plates have, but the advice is half.

quiz.p: Why must food be digested before the body can use it?
opts: Only tiny pieces can pass through the gut wall into the blood
quiz.why: Big chains like starch and protein are cut into glucose and amino acids. Only these tiny pieces pass into the blood. Picking 'food is dirty' confuses digestion with cleaning food.
quiz.context: In the Paper-Clip Journey, only single paper clips fit through the slot in the card that stands for the gut wall.

quiz.p: What do your cells do with glucose?
opts: Burn it with oxygen for energy
quiz.why: Mitochondria join glucose with oxygen and release energy. Carbon dioxide and water are left over. Picking 'store it in the bones' mixes glucose up with calcium.

quiz.p: What does iron do in the body?
quiz.why: Iron is part of the red part of blood that carries oxygen. Calcium makes bones hard. Picking 'makes bones hard' is a common mix-up between the two minerals.

quiz.p: Why does the body need some fat?
opts: It builds the thin skin around every cell, and helps us take in some vitamins
quiz.why: Every cell is wrapped in a thin skin, the cell membrane, made largely of fats. Fat also carries vitamins A, D, E and K. Picking 'it is never needed' is a common idea, but the body cannot live without some fat.

quiz.p: In the Vanishing Blue test, which result means the most vitamin C?
opts: The juice needing the fewest drops
The juice needing the most drops
The juice with the brightest colour
quiz.why: Vitamin C takes away the blue. If a few drops are enough, each drop holds a lot of vitamin C. Picking 'most drops' reads the test backwards.
quiz.context: In the Vanishing Blue test, you count drops of juice until a blue iodine and starch liquid turns clear.

quiz.p: In Balloon Bellies, every bottle had the same yeast and warm water. Only the food was different. Why?
opts: So we know the food caused the difference
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Then any difference must come from that one thing. Picking 'to use up the yeast' misses the reason for keeping things the same.
quiz.context: In Balloon Bellies, you feed yeast sugar, atta or nothing, and watch balloons fill with gas.

quiz.p: What do gut microbes mostly eat?
quiz.why: Fibre passes through to the large intestine undigested, and gut microbes feast on it. They make acids that feed our gut cells in return. Picking 'only sugar' fits the yeast in a bottle. But our own body takes up most sugar before it reaches the gut microbes.

quiz.p: Meera eats white bread and no vegetables or fruit for a whole week. What happens to her gut microbes?
opts: Many of them go hungry, because they get very little fibre
They grow more, because bread has sugar
Nothing. Gut microbes do not need food
quiz.why: Gut microbes live mostly on fibre, which comes from vegetables, fruit, dals and whole grains. White bread has little fibre, so many microbes go hungry. Our own body takes up the sugar from bread before it reaches them.

quiz.p: Your friend says 'sweets are bad food'. What does science say?
opts: No single food is good or bad. The whole diet over many days matters.
quiz.why: Scientists look at the overall pattern. Sweets give quick energy and are fine sometimes. Lots of added sugar every day is linked to tooth decay and other problems. Picking 'sweets are poison' goes far beyond the evidence.

open_questions.q: Is there one best diet for everyone?
open_questions.why_open: Very different traditional diets have kept people healthy. Scientists still argue about whether general rules or personal plans are best.

open_questions.q: How much do gut microbes affect our mood, thinking and illnesses?
open_questions.why_open: Mice with no gut microbes behave differently, and some human studies show links. But in people, cause and effect are hard to untangle, and many claims go beyond the evidence.

open_questions.q: Which fats are best for the heart, and how much of them?
open_questions.why_open: Studies disagree, partly because people eat many foods together and it is hard to test one fat for many years.

open_questions.q: Why do 'ultra-processed' foods seem to make people eat more?
open_questions.why_open: One careful 2019 test showed people ate more on such foods, but nobody yet knows exactly why: speed of eating, softness, taste or something else.

open_questions.q: Are there nutrients in food that we have not discovered yet?
open_questions.why_open: The last vitamin was found in 1948. But plants contain thousands of other substances, and scientists are still finding out what some of them do in the body.

open_questions.q: How does the body know when it has had enough of a particular nutrient?
open_questions.why_open: Animals seem to seek out protein and salt when they are low. In people, how hunger for particular foods works is only partly understood.

maths.problem: A juice box says 'Sugars: 12 grams per 100 millilitres'. The box holds 200 millilitres. A level teaspoon of sugar weighs about 4 grams. How many teaspoons of sugar are in the whole box?
maths.explain: The box is 200 millilitres, which is 2 lots of 100. So the sugar is 12 + 12 = 24 grams. Each teaspoon is 4 grams. 24 divided by 4 is 6. So there are 6 teaspoons of sugar in the box.
maths.context: In How Many Spoons?, you read the sugar on drink labels and spooned out that much sugar onto saucers.
maths.why_maths: Labels give sugar in grams, which are hard to picture. Dividing by 4 turns grams into teaspoons you can see on a saucer.

maths.problem: Your thali has 8 equal spaces. About half the plate should be vegetables and fruit. A quarter should be grains. A quarter should be dal, curd or eggs. How many spaces does each get?
maths.answer: Vegetables and fruit 4 spaces, grains 2 spaces, dal, curd or eggs 2 spaces.
maths.explain: Half of 8 is 8 divided by 2, which is 4. A quarter of 8 is 8 divided by 4, which is 2. Check: 4 + 2 + 2 = 8. All the spaces are used.
maths.context: In Build a Balanced Thali, you split your plate into one half and two quarters.
maths.why_maths: Halves and quarters turn 'eat lots of vegetables' into a plate you can actually serve.

maths.problem: In the 30-Plant Week, one leaf stands for 2 new plants. On Monday you found 10 new plants, on Tuesday 6, on Wednesday 5 and on Thursday 3. How many leaves do you draw for each day? How many plants is that so far?
maths.answer: Monday 5 leaves, Tuesday 3 leaves, Wednesday 2 and a half leaves, Thursday 1 and a half leaves. That is 24 plants so far.
maths.explain: Divide each day's plants by 2. 10 divided by 2 is 5. 6 divided by 2 is 3. 5 divided by 2 is 2 with 1 left over, so 2 and a half leaves. 3 divided by 2 is 1 with 1 left over, so 1 and a half leaves. Total plants: 10 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 24.
maths.context: In the 30-Plant Week, you counted the new plants you ate each day and drew a pictograph.
maths.why_maths: A pictograph with a key shows a week of counting at a glance, without drawing every single plant.

maths.problem: In the Vanishing Blue test, amla cleared the blue in 3 drops. Lemon needed 18 drops. About how many times more vitamin C is in a drop of amla than a drop of lemon?
maths.explain: The same amount of blue needs the same amount of vitamin C. Amla did it in 3 drops and lemon in 18. 18 divided by 3 is 6. So one drop of amla carries about as much vitamin C as 6 drops of lemon.
maths.context: In the Vanishing Blue test, you counted drops of each juice until the blue liquid turned clear.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the drop counts turns 'amla has more' into 'amla has about 6 times as much', which is a much stronger claim.

maths.problem: In Balloon Bellies, the sugar balloon was 8 cm round at 15 minutes, 17 cm at 30 minutes and 28 cm at 45 minutes. How much did it grow in each 15 minutes? Was it growing faster at the start or at the end?
maths.answer: It grew 8 cm, then 9 cm, then 11 cm. It grew fastest at the end.
maths.explain: From 0 to 8 is 8 cm. From 8 to 17 is 17 − 8 = 9 cm. From 17 to 28 is 28 − 17 = 11 cm. The growth got bigger each time, so it was fastest at the end. Dry yeast takes a while to wake up in warm water. As more of the yeast starts eating, the gas comes faster.
maths.context: In Balloon Bellies, you measured how round each balloon was every 15 minutes with a string and a ruler.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting each measurement from the next shows how fast the microbes were working, not just how big the balloon got.

deep_truth.truth: On your paper, the oil spot stayed while the water spot dried. In the tumbler, oil floated on the water and would not mix. Because fat does not mix with water, your body uses it to build the thin skin around every cell. So some of the fat you eat becomes the skin of your cells.
deep_truth.habit: We think of food as fuel, like petrol for a scooter, and of fat as something to avoid. But a scooter is not built from its petrol, and you are built from your food, fat included.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper Window Test, the water spot dried away, while oil, peanut and coconut left see-through spots that stayed. Two drops of oil in a tumbler of water floated and did not mix. Every cell membrane is made largely of fats that line up in two layers, because they do not mix with water.

three.who_am_i: Your muscles are built from amino acids that came from many foods. Some came from the rice and some from the dal.
three.what_is_life: A living body is always rebuilding itself. The lining of your gut is made new every few days, from the food you eat.
three.what_is_this_world: The world comes into you at every meal, as soil, sunlight, rain, plants, animals and other people's work.

roots.thread: Food does not stay food inside you. The fat in a peanut becomes the skin of your cells. The amino acids in dal become your muscle, and the calcium in ragi becomes your bone. So you are built, piece by piece, from many different foods, and each kind builds a different part. That is why one food, however good, can never be enough.

teachings.teaching: Yoga is not for someone who eats too much, nor for someone who does not eat at all. It is for someone who is balanced in eating, sleeping, waking and work.
teachings.link: Science also finds that health comes from balance, not from too much or too little of any one food.

teachings.source: The Buddha's first teaching, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught a middle way between living only for pleasure and harming the body by going without. Buddhist tradition says he took this path after a young woman, Sujata, gave him a bowl of rice cooked in milk, when he had almost starved himself.
teachings.link: A balanced diet is a middle way too. Neither feasting every day nor going without keeps the body well.

teachings.teaching: From food all creatures are born. By food they live, and into food they return. The Upanishad calls the body the layer of a person made of food, and says breath, mind, understanding and joy are deeper layers.
teachings.link: Science agrees about the body: your cells are built from what you eat. Whether a person is more than this body made of food is a question science cannot settle.

science.text: Every cell membrane is made largely of fats. They line up in two layers because they do not mix with water.
The body rebuilds itself from food all the time. The gut lining is replaced every few days, and red blood cells about every four months.

other_view.view: The body can make most of the fats it needs from sugar and starch. Only a few kinds of fat, called essential fatty acids, must come from food. On this view, the fat on our plate matters mostly as energy, and a small amount is plenty.

practice.title: The thank-you bite
practice.say: Let's take one small piece of chapati or a spoon of rice. Don't swallow it yet. Close your eyes and chew it slowly, thirty times. Notice how it starts to taste a little sweet. That is the enzyme in your spit cutting starch into sugar. Now swallow. Put your hand on your tummy. In a few hours, this bite will be glucose in your blood and food for your brain. Its fibre will feed the microbes in your gut. Breathe out slowly onto your other hand. Feel the warmth. Let's sit for three breaths. Think of the people who grew this food and the person who cooked it.
practice.kid: Take one small bite of chapati. Close your eyes. Chew it slowly, thirty times. Does it turn a little sweet? Swallow. Put your hand on your tummy. Think of all the cells and microbes this bite will feed. Breathe out slowly three times.

ask: The fat in a peanut can become the skin of your cells. When does the peanut stop being a peanut and start being you?
If what a food gives you depends on what you eat it with, can a food be good or bad on its own?
Your gut microbes eat the fibre that you cannot. Is that fibre food for you, or food for them?

playtest: Every flow was walked through as if done at home today. The Paper Window Test (e1) works with brown paper or plain white paper. It now says to use chapati made without ghee and to wait a full 15 minutes, because wet spots look like fat spots at first. The Vanishing Blue test (e2) was worked out with the amounts of a home bottle of povidone-iodine: about 5 to 10 drops in a cup of diluted rice water gives a blue that amla clears in a few drops and lemon or mosambi in about 20. It now says what to do if the blue is too dark or stays brown, and to stop counting at 40 drops. Balloon Bellies (e3) was changed from 1 to 2 teaspoons of yeast and from 100 to 150 millilitres of water, so the sugar balloon visibly fills within 45 minutes. It says how to check for dead yeast, and to wait to 60 minutes in cold weather. Cell Delivery (g1) was checked with a computer model of the rules. A careful player feeds all six cells in 8 turns about 4 times in 5, in 6 turns about half the time, and in 5 turns rarely. So the solo goal is 8, then 7, then 6. The water card was replaced by buttermilk plus an 'I drink water' turn, so no player can be locked out of water. What's Missing? (g2) has an answer list for every card. Parents should know that every flow avoids calling any food or family meal bad, and that the hunger scale (a6) is for noticing, never for making a child eat less. In the Paper Window Test, a tumbler of water with 2 drops of oil was added, so the child sees with their own eyes that fat does not mix with water. how_we_found_out.story: In the 1880s, many soldiers and prisoners in Java, then ruled by the Netherlands, fell ill with beriberi. Their legs grew weak and numb, and some died. Doctors were sure a germ caused the illness. In 1886 a Dutch doctor, Christiaan Eijkman, went to Java to find that germ. By luck, the chickens at his laboratory fell ill with the same kind of weakness. They were being fed leftover white rice from the hospital, with its outer layers polished off. Then a new manager stopped giving the hospital's rice to the chickens. They got cheaper unpolished rice instead, and they got better. Eijkman thought white rice carried a poison, and that the outer layer of the grain cured it. In 1901 his colleague Gerrit Grijns said the opposite. The outer layer held something the body needs, and white rice simply lacked it. Grijns was right. In 1926 two scientists in Java, Barend Jansen and Willem Donath, took the missing nutrient out of rice bran. Today we call it vitamin B1, or thiamine.
how_we_found_out.who: Christiaan Eijkman, Gerrit Grijns, Barend Jansen and Willem Donath
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Beriberi was caused by a germ, or by a poison in white rice. In fact it was caused by something missing from white rice: vitamin B1.
